lessons.title: Antonyms
lessons.html:
Antonyms

Antonyms are words or expressions that have opposite or contrasting meanings. In the JAMB Use of English examination, candidates may be required to identify the word or expression that is closest in meaning to the opposite of a given word, especially as it is used in a sentence.

Antonyms are tested under Lexis and Structure. The JAMB syllabus expects candidates to be able to determine the opposite meaning of words and expressions and to understand words in ordinary, figurative, and idiomatic contexts.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • Define an antonym correctly.
  • Distinguish antonyms from synonyms.
  • Identify common types of antonyms.
  • Determine the opposite meaning of a word from its context.
  • Recognise antonyms used in ordinary and figurative expressions.
  • Apply grammatical class, context, and register when selecting an answer.
  • Answer JAMB-style antonym questions accurately and efficiently.

1. What Is an Antonym?

An antonym is a word whose meaning is opposite or significantly different from that of another word.

For example:

  • hot — cold
  • early — late
  • ancient — modern
  • accept — reject
  • victory — defeat
  • expand — contract

The important point is that the relationship between the two words is one of contrast or opposition.

Antonyms Compared with Synonyms

A synonym has a similar meaning to another word, while an antonym has an opposite or contrasting meaning.

WordSynonymAntonym
bravecourageouscowardly
ancientoldmodern
rapidfastslow
generousliberalstingy
permitallowforbid

2. Types of Antonyms

Understanding different types of opposites helps you recognise antonyms even when the relationship is not simply between two obvious opposites.

A. Gradable Antonyms

Gradable antonyms are opposites that exist at different points on a scale. There can be degrees between them.

Examples include:

  • hot — cold
  • big — small
  • rich — poor
  • fast — slow
  • young — old

There can be intermediate degrees. Something may be warm without being either extremely hot or extremely cold.

B. Complementary Antonyms

Complementary antonyms present two mutually exclusive conditions. If one applies, the other normally does not.

Examples include:

  • alive — dead
  • present — absent
  • true — false
  • legal — illegal
  • married — unmarried

C. Relational or Converse Antonyms

These words describe opposite relationships or perspectives involving the same situation.

Examples include:

  • buy — sell
  • give — receive
  • lend — borrow
  • employer — employee
  • teacher — student

For example, if Musa buys a book from Ada, Ada sells the book to Musa. The two words describe opposite sides of the same transaction.

3. Antonyms and Word Classes

When answering an antonym question, first identify the grammatical class of the word being tested. The best opposite will normally belong to the same grammatical class.

Word ClassExampleAntonym
Nounsuccessfailure
Verbacceptreject
Adjectivegenerousstingy
Adverbcarefullycarelessly

For example, if the question asks for the opposite of carefully, an answer such as carelessly is grammatically appropriate, whereas carelessness is a noun and does not fit the same grammatical position.

4. Antonyms in Context

One of the most important skills in JAMB Use of English is recognising that a word can have different meanings depending on how it is used. Therefore, do not select an antonym simply because it is listed as an opposite in a dictionary. Read the complete sentence first.

Example 1: Ordinary Meaning

Question: The manager was generous to his workers.

Possible opposite: stingy

Here, generous means willing to give or share freely. Its appropriate opposite is stingy or mean, depending on the options provided.

Example 2: Context Changes the Choice

Question: The witness gave a vague account of the incident.

Possible opposite: clear

In this sentence, vague means unclear or lacking precise details. Therefore, clear is a suitable opposite.

Example 3: Verb in Context

Question: The chairman approved the proposal.

Possible opposite: rejected

Here, approved means accepted or officially agreed to something. Its opposite in the sentence is rejected.

5. Ordinary, Figurative and Idiomatic Usage

JAMB may test words and expressions in ordinary, figurative, or idiomatic contexts. The meaning you choose must therefore agree with the way the expression is used in the sentence.

Ordinary Usage

In ordinary usage, a word generally has its direct and common meaning.

Example: The water is shallow.

The opposite of shallow in this context is deep.

Figurative Usage

In figurative usage, a word may communicate an idea beyond its literal meaning.

Example: The politician is known for his cold attitude towards criticism.

Here, cold does not refer to temperature. It means unfriendly or unemotional. An appropriate opposite is warm or friendly, depending on the options.

Idiomatic Usage

An idiom is an expression whose overall meaning cannot always be understood simply by interpreting each word literally.

When an idiomatic expression appears in a question, consider the meaning of the expression as a whole rather than trying to find a literal opposite for one word.

Example: After losing the contract, the businessman was down in the dumps.

The expression down in the dumps means very unhappy or depressed. An appropriate opposite in context could be cheerful or happy.

6. Prefixes and Antonyms

Some opposites are formed by adding prefixes to words. Common negative or reversing prefixes include un-, in-, im-, il-, ir-, dis-, and non-.

WordOpposite
happyunhappy
correctincorrect
possibleimpossible
legalillegal
regularirregular
honestdishonest

However, do not assume that simply adding a negative prefix always produces the exact answer required. The sentence context remains important.

7. Common Antonym Pairs for JAMB Preparation

The following pairs are useful for vocabulary development:

WordAntonym
abundantscarce
ancientmodern
artificialnatural
boldtimid
brieflengthy
carefulcareless
concealreveal
createdestroy
defendattack
diminishincrease
domesticforeign
expandcontract
flexiblerigid
frequentrare
genuinefake
hostilefriendly
humblearrogant
inferiorsuperior
innocentguilty
libertycaptivity
maximumminimum
permanenttemporary
permitforbid
plentifulscarce
precisevague
prosperitypoverty
rigidflexible
ruralurban
transparentopaque
victorydefeat

8. How to Answer JAMB Antonym Questions

Step 1: Read the Whole Sentence

Do not focus only on the underlined word. Read the complete sentence because the surrounding words often reveal the intended meaning.

Step 2: Determine the Meaning in Context

Ask yourself what the word means in that particular sentence. A word may have more than one meaning.

Step 3: Identify the Word Class

Determine whether the tested word is a noun, verb, adjective, adverb, or another grammatical form. This helps eliminate unsuitable options.

Step 4: Think of an Opposite

Before looking closely at the options, mentally supply an opposite. This prevents you from being distracted by words that are related but not truly opposite.

Step 5: Compare the Options

Check which option expresses the strongest and most appropriate opposite meaning in the given context.

Step 6: Check the Grammar

Insert the selected answer into the sentence mentally. Make sure it fits grammatically and makes logical sense.

9. Common Traps in Antonym Questions

Trap 1: Choosing a Related Word

A word may be related to the tested word without being its opposite.

Example: If the word is wealthy, money is related to wealth but is not its antonym. The appropriate opposite is poor or impoverished, depending on the context.

Trap 2: Ignoring the Context

A word may have several meanings. Always identify the meaning intended by the sentence before selecting an opposite.

Trap 3: Confusing Synonyms with Antonyms

If the question asks for the opposite of rapid, choosing fast is incorrect because fast is similar in meaning to rapid. The expected opposite is slow.

Trap 4: Ignoring Grammatical Form

The answer should normally fit the same grammatical position as the tested word. For example, the opposite of the adjective generous should normally be another adjective such as stingy, not the noun stinginess.

Trap 5: Selecting an Extreme Opposite

Some words have gradable meanings. The best answer may be the natural contextual opposite rather than an unnecessarily extreme word.

10. Worked Examples

Example 1

Question: The instructions were explicit.

What is the opposite of explicit?

  1. A. clear
  2. B. definite
  3. C. vague
  4. D. precise

Answer: C. vague

Explanation: Explicit means clearly expressed or stated. Vague means unclear or not precisely expressed, making it the appropriate opposite.

Example 2

Question: The chairman decided to approve the proposal.

What is the opposite of approve?

  1. A. accept
  2. B. reject
  3. C. support
  4. D. endorse

Answer: B. reject

Explanation: To approve something is to accept or officially agree to it. To reject it is to refuse or decline to accept it.

Example 3

Question: The village experienced abundant rainfall.

What is the opposite of abundant?

  1. A. heavy
  2. B. sufficient
  3. C. scarce
  4. D. regular

Answer: C. scarce

Explanation: Abundant means available in large quantities, while scarce means available in insufficient or small quantities.

Example 4

Question: The witness gave a credible account of the incident.

What is the opposite of credible?

  1. A. convincing
  2. B. reliable
  3. C. unbelievable
  4. D. accurate

Answer: C. unbelievable

Explanation: Credible means believable or worthy of trust. Therefore, unbelievable gives the appropriate opposite meaning.

11. Practice Questions

Choose the option that is nearest in meaning to the opposite of the word or expression in bold.

Question 1

The new policy is intended to promote economic growth.

  1. A. encourage
  2. B. support
  3. C. hinder
  4. D. develop

Question 2

The principal praised the student's diligent attitude.

  1. A. hardworking
  2. B. careless
  3. C. serious
  4. D. careful

Question 3

The man's explanation was plausible.

  1. A. reasonable
  2. B. convincing
  3. C. unlikely
  4. D. acceptable

Question 4

The committee reached a unanimous decision.

  1. A. collective
  2. B. divided
  3. C. complete
  4. D. final

Question 5

The manager was reluctant to approve the request.

  1. A. unwilling
  2. B. hesitant
  3. C. eager
  4. D. doubtful

Question 6

The candidate gave a concise answer.

  1. A. brief
  2. B. lengthy
  3. C. direct
  4. D. simple

Question 7

The evidence was conclusive.

  1. A. decisive
  2. B. convincing
  3. C. inconclusive
  4. D. sufficient

Question 8

The company's profits have increased significantly.

  1. A. improved
  2. B. declined
  3. C. expanded
  4. D. developed

12. Answers to Practice Questions

  1. C — hinder: To promote is to encourage or help something to develop; to hinder is to obstruct or prevent progress.
  2. B — careless: Diligent means hardworking and careful, while careless expresses the opposite quality.
  3. C — unlikely: Plausible means reasonable or believable; unlikely expresses the opposite idea in this context.
  4. B — divided: Unanimous means involving complete agreement, while divided indicates disagreement or lack of unity.
  5. C — eager: Reluctant means unwilling or hesitant, while eager means very willing or enthusiastic.
  6. B — lengthy: Concise means brief and expressed using few words; lengthy means long or extended.
  7. C — inconclusive: Conclusive means decisive or settling an issue; inconclusive means not producing a definite conclusion.
  8. B — declined: Increased means became greater, while declined means became smaller or decreased.

13. JAMB Examination Strategy

Antonym questions can often be answered quickly if you use a systematic approach. First identify the meaning of the tested word in the sentence. Next identify its grammatical class. Then eliminate options that are synonyms, merely related words, or grammatically unsuitable. Finally, choose the option that gives the most natural opposite meaning in context.

Do not rely exclusively on memorised word pairs. JAMB may place a familiar word in an unfamiliar context, so your ability to interpret the sentence is more important than simply recalling a list of opposites.

Quick Elimination Method

  • Eliminate synonyms: Remove options that have a similar meaning to the tested word.
  • Eliminate unrelated words: A word may belong to the same topic without being an opposite.
  • Check grammar: Make sure the option can occupy the same grammatical position.
  • Check context: Select the opposite meaning that fits the sentence.
  • Check register: Prefer an answer that matches the level and style of the original expression.

14. Summary

An antonym is a word or expression that has an opposite or contrasting meaning to another word or expression. JAMB tests antonyms as part of Lexis and Structure and may require candidates to understand opposite meanings in ordinary, figurative, and idiomatic contexts.

To answer antonym questions successfully, always consider context, grammatical class, precise meaning, and the relationship between the options. Avoid choosing an answer merely because it is related to the tested word.

Remember: The correct antonym is the option that gives the most appropriate opposite meaning in the particular sentence.

15. Self-Assessment Checklist

Before leaving this lesson, you should be able to answer Yes to the following:

  • I can define an antonym.
  • I can distinguish antonyms from synonyms.
  • I can recognise gradable, complementary, and relational opposites.
  • I can identify the word class of a tested word.
  • I can determine an antonym from context.
  • I understand that words may have different meanings in different contexts.
  • I can recognise ordinary, figurative, and idiomatic usage.
  • I can eliminate distractors in JAMB-style antonym questions.
  • I can select an answer based on precise contextual meaning rather than simple word association.

lessons.html:
Clause, Sentence Patterns and Word Classes

Understanding clauses, sentence patterns and word classes is essential for answering many questions in English Language. These areas help you identify how words function in a sentence, how sentences are constructed and how meaning is communicated correctly.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • define a clause and distinguish it from a phrase;
  • identify the subject and predicate of a clause;
  • distinguish between independent and dependent clauses;
  • identify the major types of clauses and their functions;
  • recognise simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences;
  • identify common sentence patterns;
  • identify and classify the major word classes in English;
  • distinguish between words that look similar but perform different grammatical functions; and
  • apply these concepts when answering objective questions.

1. What Is a Clause?

A clause is a group of words that contains a subject and a verb. The verb in a clause normally shows what the subject does, what happens to the subject or the state of the subject.

Examples:

  • The students arrived. — subject: the students; verb: arrived.
  • She is reading. — subject: she; verb phrase: is reading.
  • because the students arrived — subject: the students; verb: arrived.

Notice that the last example contains a subject and a verb, so it is a clause, but it does not express a complete thought by itself.

2. Clause and Phrase

A phrase is a group of related words that does not contain a subject-verb relationship that forms a clause. A clause, on the other hand, contains a subject and a verb.

ExpressionTypeReason
in the morningPhraseNo subject-verb relationship
after the examinationPhraseNo subject-verb relationship
when the examination endedClauseContains subject the examination and verb ended
the examination endedClauseContains subject and verb

Examination tip: When asked to identify a clause, look first for a subject and a verb. Do not assume that every group of words is a clause.

3. Independent and Dependent Clauses

Independent Clause

An independent clause expresses a complete thought and can stand alone as a sentence.

Examples:

  • The candidate passed the examination.
  • We arrived early.
  • She works very hard.

Dependent Clause

A dependent clause, also called a subordinate clause, contains a subject and a verb but does not express a complete thought on its own. It depends on another clause to complete its meaning.

Examples:

  • because the candidate passed
  • when we arrived
  • although she worked hard

These expressions need another clause to form a complete sentence:

Although she worked hard, she did not pass the examination.

4. Types of Clauses According to Function

Dependent clauses can perform different grammatical functions in a sentence. The major types commonly tested include noun clauses, adjective or relative clauses and adverbial clauses.

Noun Clause

A noun clause performs a function normally performed by a noun. It may serve as the subject, object or complement of a sentence.

Examples:

  • What he said was true. — The clause is the subject.
  • I know that she is honest. — The clause is the object of know.
  • The problem is that we are late. — The clause functions as a complement.

Common introductory words include that, what, whatever, who, whoever, whether and how, depending on the construction.

Adjective or Relative Clause

An adjective clause, also called a relative clause, modifies or describes a noun or pronoun.

Examples:

  • The student who won the prize is my friend.
  • I read the book which you recommended.
  • The house that Jack built is beautiful.

The words who, whom, whose, which and that frequently introduce relative clauses.

Adverbial Clause

An adverbial clause performs the function of an adverb. It may tell us when, where, why, how, under what condition or despite what circumstance something happens.

Examples:

  • We left when the rain stopped. — time
  • He stayed at home because he was ill. — reason
  • If you work hard, you will succeed. — condition
  • Although he was tired, he continued working. — concession

5. Main and Subordinate Clauses

The main clause carries the principal idea of the sentence and can usually stand alone. A subordinate clause depends on the main clause.

Example:

When the bell rang, the students left the classroom.

  • Subordinate clause: When the bell rang
  • Main clause: the students left the classroom

A useful test is to ask whether the clause can stand alone and still express a complete thought.

6. Sentence Structure

A sentence is a grammatically complete unit of expression. Sentences can be classified according to the number and relationship of their clauses.

Simple Sentence

A simple sentence contains one independent clause. It may contain a compound subject or compound predicate but still has only one independent clause.

Examples:

  • Amina reads every evening.
  • Amina and Tunde read every evening.
  • Amina reads and writes every evening.

The presence of more than one verb does not automatically make a sentence compound. The important question is whether there is more than one independent clause.

Compound Sentence

A compound sentence contains two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction or suitable punctuation.

Common coordinating conjunctions are for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.

Examples:

  • I studied hard, and I passed the examination.
  • She was tired, but she continued working.
  • Hurry up, or you will miss the bus.

Complex Sentence

A complex sentence contains one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.

Examples:

  • Although he was tired, he continued working.
  • We waited until the teacher arrived.
  • If you practise regularly, your performance will improve.

Compound-Complex Sentence

A compound-complex sentence contains at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause.

Example:

Although he was tired, he continued working, and his sister prepared the meal.

In this sentence, Although he was tired is dependent, while he continued working and his sister prepared the meal are independent clauses.

7. Sentence Patterns

Sentence patterns describe the basic arrangement of grammatical elements in a sentence. The common elements are Subject (S), Verb (V), Object (O), Complement (C) and Adverbial (A).

Subject + Verb (S + V)

The subject performs the action or exists in the stated condition.

  • The baby cried.
  • The students laughed.
  • Birds fly.

Subject + Verb + Object (S + V + O)

The object receives the action of the verb.

  • The boy kicked the ball.
  • She opened the door.
  • The teacher praised the student.

Subject + Verb + Complement (S + V + C)

A complement completes the meaning of a linking verb by identifying or describing the subject.

  • She is a doctor.
  • The soup tastes delicious.
  • He became angry.

Common linking verbs include be, become, seem, appear, feel, look, smell, taste and remain, although their exact function depends on context.

Subject + Verb + Indirect Object + Direct Object (S + V + IO + DO)

Some verbs can take two objects. The indirect object normally identifies the receiver or beneficiary, while the direct object identifies what is given, sent or shown.

  • She gave the boy a book.
  • The teacher taught us English.
  • My father bought me a bicycle.

Subject + Verb + Object + Complement (S + V + O + C)

The complement describes or identifies the object.

  • They elected him president.
  • The news made her happy.
  • We found the room empty.

Subject + Verb + Adverbial (S + V + A)

Some sentence patterns include an adverbial element that gives information about place, time, manner or another circumstance.

  • She lives in Lagos.
  • The children stayed at home.
  • The meeting begins at noon.

8. Word Classes

Word classes are categories into which words are grouped according to their form and grammatical function. The major word classes include nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions, determiners and interjections.

Nouns

A noun names a person, animal, place, thing, substance, activity, quality or idea.

Examples include teacher, Nigeria, table, water, honesty, education and committee.

Nouns may be classified as common, proper, concrete, abstract, collective, countable or uncountable, depending on the basis of classification.

Pronouns

A pronoun is used in place of a noun or noun phrase to avoid unnecessary repetition.

Examples include I, you, he, she, it, we, they, me, him, her, them, who, which, someone and themselves.

Example: Chika said Chika would come can be improved to Chika said she would come.

Verbs

A verb expresses an action, event, process or state.

Examples include run, write, think, become, know, exist and is.

Verbs may be classified in different ways, including main verbs and auxiliary verbs. Auxiliary verbs help form tense, aspect, voice, questions and other grammatical constructions.

Examples of auxiliary verbs include be, have, do, can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must and ought to.

Adjectives

An adjective modifies a noun or pronoun by describing, identifying or limiting it.

Examples:

  • a beautiful house
  • a difficult question
  • the three candidates

In The boy is intelligent, intelligent is an adjective functioning as a subject complement.

Adverbs

An adverb modifies a verb, adjective, another adverb or sometimes an entire clause. It may express manner, time, place, frequency, degree or viewpoint.

Examples:

  • She spoke slowly. — manner
  • He arrived yesterday. — time
  • They live nearby. — place
  • She often visits us. — frequency
  • The question is very difficult. — degree

Prepositions

A preposition usually shows a relationship between a noun or pronoun and another element in the sentence. It may express place, time, direction, cause or other relationships.

Examples include in, on, at, by, for, from, with, under, over, between, among, through, during and after.

Examples:

  • The book is on the table.
  • We arrived after lunch.
  • She travelled from Abuja.

Conjunctions

Conjunctions connect words, phrases or clauses.

Coordinating conjunctions join units of equal grammatical status, for example and, but, or, nor, for, so and yet.

Subordinating conjunctions introduce dependent clauses. Examples include because, although, if, unless, when, while, since, before, after and until.

Correlative conjunctions occur in pairs, such as either...or, neither...nor, both...and, not only...but also.

Determiners

Determiners occur before nouns and help identify or limit their reference. Examples include articles, demonstratives, possessives and certain quantifiers.

Examples include a, an, the, this, that, these, those, my, your, some, many, each and every.

Example: Those students submitted their assignments.

Interjections

An interjection is a word or expression used to express a sudden feeling or reaction.

Examples include oh, wow, alas, ah, hey and hurrah.

Example: Wow! That was an excellent performance.

9. The Importance of Context

A word should not always be classified solely by its dictionary meaning. Its grammatical function in the sentence is important.

For example, fast can function as an adjective in a fast car and as an adverb in He runs fast.

Similarly, before can function differently according to context:

  • before the examination — preposition
  • before we arrived — conjunction introducing a clause
  • I had seen him before — adverb

Key principle: In objective questions, identify what the word is doing in the particular sentence rather than relying only on what the word normally means.

10. Common Examination Traps

  • Confusing a phrase with a clause: Check whether the group contains a subject and a verb.
  • Assuming every sentence with two verbs is compound: Determine whether the verbs belong to separate independent clauses.
  • Confusing an adjective with an adverb: Identify the word being modified.
  • Ignoring context: The same word can belong to different word classes in different sentences.
  • Confusing object and complement: An object receives the action, while a complement completes or describes the subject or object.
  • Misidentifying dependent clauses: Words such as although, because, if, when and unless often introduce subordinate clauses.

11. Quick Identification Strategy

When faced with a question on this topic, use the following approach:

  1. Read the entire sentence before analysing the target word or expression.
  2. Find the main verb or verb phrase.
  3. Identify the subject associated with the verb.
  4. Determine whether the expression is a phrase or a clause.
  5. If it is a clause, determine whether it is independent or dependent.
  6. For a dependent clause, ask whether it functions as a noun, adjective or adverb.
  7. For a word-class question, determine what the target word modifies or what function it performs.
  8. For a sentence-pattern question, identify the subject, verb, object, complement and adverbial elements.

12. Worked Examples

Example 1

Question: Identify the clause in the sentence: The students who arrived early entered the hall.

Answer: who arrived early is an adjective or relative clause because it describes the students.

Example 2

Question: What type of sentence is this? Although it was raining, we went to school.

Answer: It is a complex sentence because it contains one dependent clause, Although it was raining, and one independent clause, we went to school.

Example 3

Question: Identify the word class of quickly in: She completed the assignment quickly.

Answer: Quickly is an adverb because it modifies the verb completed by indicating manner.

Example 4

Question: Identify the pattern in: The teacher gave the students books.

Answer: The pattern is S + V + IO + DO. The teacher is the subject, gave is the verb, the students is the indirect object and books is the direct object.

13. Self-Test

Choose the option that best answers each question.

  1. Which of the following is a clause?
    A. after the examination
    B. in the classroom
    C. because she was late
    D. with great care
  2. In the sentence The man who lives next door is a doctor, the expression who lives next door is a/an:
    A. noun clause
    B. adjective clause
    C. adverbial clause
    D. main clause
  3. Which sentence is a compound sentence?
    A. When he arrived, we left.
    B. He arrived early because he was worried.
    C. He arrived early, and we welcomed him.
    D. Although he was tired, he continued.
  4. What is the pattern of The boy kicked the ball?
    A. S + V
    B. S + V + C
    C. S + V + O
    D. S + V + IO + DO
  5. In She speaks softly, the word softly is a/an:
    A. adjective
    B. adverb
    C. noun
    D. preposition
  6. Which of the following is a subordinating conjunction?
    A. and
    B. but
    C. because
    D. or
  7. In Honesty is important, the word Honesty is a:
    A. verb
    B. pronoun
    C. noun
    D. adjective
  8. Which sentence contains a subject complement?
    A. Musa opened the door.
    B. Musa is a doctor.
    C. Musa bought a book.
    D. Musa kicked the ball.
  9. In We arrived before the teacher, the word before functions as a:
    A. preposition
    B. adjective
    C. pronoun
    D. interjection
  10. Which sentence is complex?
    A. John came and Peter left.
    B. John came early.
    C. Because John came early, we started the meeting.
    D. John came early, and Peter left.

14. Answers to the Self-Test

  1. C — because she was late contains a subject and a verb and is a dependent clause.
  2. B — who lives next door modifies the noun man.
  3. C — It contains two independent clauses joined by and.
  4. C — The boy is S, kicked is V and the ball is O.
  5. B — softly modifies the verb speaks.
  6. C — because introduces a dependent clause.
  7. C — Honesty names an abstract quality and is therefore a noun.
  8. B — a doctor identifies the subject after the linking verb is.
  9. A — before is followed by the noun phrase the teacher.
  10. C — It contains one dependent clause and one independent clause.

15. Summary

A clause contains a subject and a verb. An independent clause can stand alone, while a dependent clause cannot. Dependent clauses may function as nouns, adjectives or adverbs. Sentences may be simple, compound, complex or compound-complex depending on their clause structure.

Sentence patterns show how grammatical elements such as subjects, verbs, objects, complements and adverbials are arranged. Common patterns include S + V, S + V + O, S + V + C, S + V + IO + DO, S + V + O + C and S + V + A.

Word classes classify words according to their grammatical behaviour and function. Major classes include nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions, determiners and interjections.

Remember: In examination questions, always analyse the word or clause in its context. Do not depend only on its dictionary definition or appearance.

lessons.title: Cloze Tests and Contextual Meaning
lessons.html:
Cloze Tests and Contextual Meaning

A cloze test is a passage in which some words have been removed and replaced with gaps. The candidate is required to choose the word or expression that best completes each gap. In the JAMB Use of English examination, cloze passages test more than the ability to recognise individual words. You must understand the meaning, grammar, relationships between ideas and overall direction of the passage.

The official JAMB Use of English syllabus identifies one of the two comprehension passages as a cloze test. It also states that questions may test comprehension of the whole or part of a passage, the meaning of words and expressions as used in context, coherence, logical reasoning, deductions and inferences. Therefore, successful performance requires you to read the passage as a connected unit rather than treating each gap as an isolated question.

What Is Contextual Meaning?

Contextual meaning is the meaning a word or expression takes from the sentence and passage in which it occurs. A word may have several dictionary meanings, but only one meaning may be suitable in a particular context.

For example, the word “bright” can describe light, intelligence, colour or a promising future. In the sentence, “The student is very bright,” the word means intelligent. In “The room was bright,” it refers to the amount of light. The surrounding words determine the intended meaning.

What JAMB Tests in Cloze Passages

Cloze questions may require you to apply several language skills at the same time. You should be prepared to test each option against the grammar, meaning and structure of the passage.

  • Comprehension: Understand what the sentence and the passage are saying.
  • Vocabulary: Select a word whose meaning is appropriate to the context.
  • Grammar: Choose a word that performs the required grammatical function.
  • Collocation: Recognise words that naturally occur together in standard English.
  • Coherence: Ensure that the selected word maintains a logical connection between ideas.
  • Inference: Use information elsewhere in the passage to determine what belongs in the gap.
  • Register: Select a word suitable for the level of formality and subject matter of the passage.

The Three Main Checks

When deciding what belongs in a gap, use three major checks: grammar, meaning and collocation.

1. Grammar

First, determine what type of word the sentence requires. The gap may need a noun, verb, adjective, adverb, pronoun, conjunction, preposition, article or another grammatical form.

Consider the sentence:

“The committee has _____ its decision.”

The word after has should be a past participle. Therefore, options such as review or reviewing would not fit this structure, while reviewed can.

Grammar can immediately eliminate options that cannot fit the sentence structure.

2. Meaning

After checking grammar, ask whether the option makes sense in the context. An answer may be grammatically correct but logically wrong.

For example:

“The heavy rain _____ the football match.”

The verb should express what heavy rain can logically cause. “Cancelled” makes sense in this context, while “celebrated” does not.

3. Collocation

Collocation refers to the natural combination of words in English. Some words regularly occur together, and JAMB may test your ability to recognise these combinations.

Examples include:

  • make a decision, not normally do a decision
  • commit a crime, not normally make a crime
  • heavy rain, not normally strong rain
  • pay attention, not normally give attention in the same construction
  • depend on, not depend at

When two or more options appear grammatically possible, collocation can help identify the most natural answer.

Read the Whole Passage

One of the most important rules in a cloze test is not to treat each gap independently. The answer to one gap may depend on information appearing several sentences later.

Read the passage once to understand its general subject and direction. Then return to the gaps and examine the surrounding sentences. Look for repeated ideas, explanations, contrasts, examples and conclusions that provide clues.

Words such as however, therefore, although, because, consequently, similarly and while are especially useful because they show relationships between ideas.

Using Immediate Context

The words immediately before and after a gap often provide the first clue. Examine the sentence carefully before considering the answer choices.

For example:

“The teacher was impressed _____ the student's improvement.”

The verb phrase “impressed by” requires the preposition by. Knowledge of the grammatical pattern helps you select the correct option.

Using Wider Context

Sometimes the immediate sentence does not provide enough information. In such cases, examine the sentences before and after it.

Suppose a passage discusses how regular exercise improves physical fitness and then says:

“For this reason, doctors often _____ their patients to exercise regularly.”

The phrase “For this reason” connects the sentence to the previous idea. Since the passage has established the benefits of exercise, the appropriate verb is one meaning to advise or recommend, such as “encourage”.

Recognising Contrast

Some gaps require an answer that signals contrast. Look for expressions such as but, however, although, despite, nevertheless and whereas.

Example:

“The first experiment was unsuccessful. _____, the researchers did not abandon the project.”

The second sentence contrasts with the first. A connector such as “However” is appropriate because it introduces an opposing or unexpected development.

Recognising Cause and Effect

Many cloze passages contain cause-and-effect relationships. Words such as because, since, therefore, thus, consequently and as a result can signal these relationships.

Example:

“The road was flooded; _____, motorists were advised to use another route.”

The second statement is a result of the first, so a result connector such as “therefore” or “consequently” fits the context.

Grammar Patterns Commonly Tested

Pay attention to grammatical structures around the gap. Certain words require particular forms or prepositions.

  • Verb + preposition: depend on, insist on, agree with, belong to.
  • Adjective + preposition: interested in, afraid of, responsible for, proud of.
  • Verb + infinitive: decide to go, hope to succeed, plan to study.
  • Verb + gerund: avoid making, enjoy reading, consider leaving.
  • Modal + base verb: can go, should study, must obey.
  • Article + noun: a book, an examination, the teacher.

Subject-Verb Agreement

A gap may require a verb that agrees with its subject. Do not allow words between the subject and verb to distract you.

Example:

“The quality of the products _____ improved.”

The subject is “quality”, which is singular, not “products”. Therefore, the correct verb is “has”: “The quality of the products has improved.”

Pronouns and Reference

A cloze question may test whether you can identify what a pronoun refers to. Words such as he, she, it, they, this, that and these must agree with and logically refer to something already mentioned.

Example:

“The committee submitted its report after _____ had completed the investigation.”

The pronoun “it” refers to the committee, while “its” shows possession.

Choosing Between Similar Words

Do not assume that two words with similar dictionary meanings can always replace each other. Their grammatical behaviour, collocations and contexts may differ.

For example, “borrow” means to receive something temporarily from another person, while “lend” means to give something temporarily to another person.

Compare:

  • “I borrowed a book from Musa.”
  • “Musa lent me a book.”

The surrounding structure determines which word is appropriate.

Eliminating Wrong Options

You do not always need to identify the answer immediately. Elimination is a useful strategy. Examine each option and ask whether it fails grammatically, semantically or contextually.

If an option is grammatically impossible, remove it. If it fits grammatically but contradicts the passage, remove it. If two options remain, compare their collocations, register and precise meanings.

A Step-by-Step JAMB Strategy

  1. Read the entire passage: Identify the subject, purpose and general tone.
  2. Read each sentence containing a gap: Examine the words immediately surrounding the gap.
  3. Predict the answer: Before looking closely at the options, think about the type of word or idea required.
  4. Check grammar: Confirm that the option fits the grammatical structure.
  5. Check meaning: Ask whether the option makes logical sense.
  6. Check collocation: Determine whether the combination of words is natural in standard English.
  7. Check the wider passage: Make sure the answer agrees with the overall argument or narrative.
  8. Use elimination: Remove options that fail any of the checks.
  9. Read the completed sentence again: Ensure that it sounds natural and preserves the intended meaning.

Worked Example

Read the passage below:

“Many students believe that success in an examination depends entirely on intelligence. This belief is not completely correct. Although intelligence is important, proper preparation is equally _____ (A) significant (B) significance (C) signify (D) significantly. A student who studies regularly is more likely to understand the material and _____ (A) retain (B) retention (C) retained (D) retaining) what has been learnt.”

Gap One

The sentence contains the phrase “is equally _____”. After the linking verb “is”, an adjective is required. “Significant” is an adjective, so it fits both the grammar and meaning of the sentence.

Answer: significant.

Gap Two

The structure is “is more likely to understand ... and _____”. The word following “to” must be a base-form verb. “Retain” fits the structure and means to keep the information in memory.

Answer: retain.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Choosing the most familiar word: Familiarity does not guarantee contextual correctness.
  • Ignoring the whole passage: A later sentence may provide the decisive clue.
  • Focusing only on grammar: A grammatically correct word may still be inappropriate in meaning.
  • Ignoring collocation: Some combinations are grammatically possible but unnatural in standard English.
  • Confusing similar words: Words such as affect/effect, borrow/lend, advice/advise and principal/principle have different uses.
  • Overthinking simple clues: When grammar, meaning and context clearly point to one answer, do not replace it merely because another option looks more sophisticated.

Practice Passage

Read the passage carefully and choose the most appropriate option for each gap.

“Education plays an important role in the development of a nation. It provides individuals with knowledge and skills that can help them _____ (1) effectively in society. However, education does not end when a person leaves school. People must continue to learn because the world is constantly ____ (2). New technologies and ideas appear regularly, and those who fail to adapt may find it difficult to _____ (3) with changing demands. For this reason, lifelong learning should be regarded as an essential part of personal and professional ____ (4).”

  • (1) A. participate   B. participation   C. participating   D. participated
  • (2) A. change   B. changing   C. changed   D. changes
  • (3) A. keep   B. hold   C. stay   D. remain
  • (4) A. develop   B. development   C. developed   D. developing

Answers and Explanations

1. Participate

The structure is “help them _____ effectively”. After “help them”, the base form of the verb is required. Participate also fits the meaning because education can help people take part effectively in society.

Correct answer: A. participate.

2. Changing

The expression “is constantly changing” is a natural grammatical structure. The adverb “constantly” indicates an ongoing process.

Correct answer: B. changing.

3. Keep

The natural collocation is “keep up with changing demands.” Among the options, keep forms the required expression.

Correct answer: A. keep.

4. Development

The phrase “personal and professional development” is a standard collocation. A noun is also required after “professional.”

Correct answer: B. development.

Quick Revision Checklist

Before submitting an answer in a cloze test, ask yourself:

  • Does the answer fit the grammar of the sentence?
  • Does it express the correct meaning?
  • Does it fit naturally with the surrounding words?
  • Does it agree with the ideas in the wider passage?
  • Have I considered clues from sentences before and after the gap?
  • Have I eliminated options that are grammatically or logically impossible?

Key Takeaway

A successful cloze-test candidate does not simply look for a word that can fit a blank. The candidate considers the entire context. The best answer is the one that satisfies grammar, meaning, collocation and the logical development of the passage. Read beyond the gap, use the information supplied by the writer, and always check the completed sentence against the overall meaning of the passage.

JAMB Syllabus Alignment

This lesson is aligned with the official JAMB Use of English syllabus, which places cloze testing within Comprehension/Summary and requires candidates to understand passages, interpret words and expressions in context, recognise coherence and logical relationships, make deductions and inferences, and identify grammatical functions. Candidates should therefore practise cloze passages as complete units of meaning rather than as isolated vocabulary questions.

lessons.title: Comprehension: Main Ideas, Inference and Vocabulary in Context
lessons.html:
Comprehension

Comprehension is the ability to read a passage, understand its meaning, identify the writer's ideas and draw conclusions that are supported by the passage. In the JAMB Use of English examination, comprehension questions test how well you understand information presented in a passage rather than how much of the passage you can memorize.

A comprehension question may require you to identify the main idea, determine the writer's purpose, understand a particular statement, make an inference, identify the meaning of a word or expression in context, determine what a pronoun refers to, or select a conclusion that is supported by the passage.

What to Look for in a Passage

Before answering questions, identify the central subject of the passage and determine what the writer is saying about that subject. The subject is the general topic, while the main idea is the most important point the writer makes about it.

For example, a passage may discuss the use of technology in education. The subject is technology in education, but the main idea might be that technology can improve learning when it is used appropriately by teachers and students.

Main Idea

The main idea is the central message or controlling point of a passage. Other sentences normally provide explanations, examples, evidence, descriptions or illustrations that support the main idea.

When a question asks for the main idea, choose the option that covers the passage as a whole. Do not choose an option that represents only one example or one minor detail.

How to Identify the Main Idea

  1. Ask yourself what the passage is mainly about.
  2. Ask what the writer wants the reader to understand about the subject.
  3. Look for ideas that are repeated or developed throughout the passage.
  4. Pay attention to the opening and concluding sentences, because they may introduce or summarize the central idea.
  5. Reject an option that is too narrow and applies to only one part of the passage.

Topic Sentence and Supporting Details

A topic sentence introduces the main point of a paragraph. Supporting details explain, prove, illustrate or develop that point. A topic sentence may appear at the beginning, middle or end of a paragraph, and sometimes the main idea has to be inferred from several sentences.

For example, if a paragraph explains that regular reading improves vocabulary, develops concentration and increases knowledge, its main point is likely to be that regular reading has several educational benefits.

Inference

An inference is a reasonable conclusion that can be drawn from information contained in the passage. An inferred answer may not be stated word-for-word, but the evidence in the passage must support it.

To make an inference, combine what the writer says with what logically follows from those statements. An inference is not a guess based on personal opinion or outside knowledge.

Example of an Inference

Suppose a passage states that a farmer planted his crops early because the weather forecast predicted heavy rainfall later in the month. We can reasonably infer that the farmer wanted the crops to receive sufficient water or to take advantage of favourable conditions before the expected heavy rainfall.

However, we cannot infer that the farmer will definitely have a successful harvest unless the passage provides evidence for that conclusion.

Rules for Answering Inference Questions

  1. Base your answer only on information supplied by the passage.
  2. Choose the conclusion that follows logically from the evidence.
  3. Do not introduce personal opinions or outside facts.
  4. Be careful with extreme expressions such as always, never, all and none.
  5. If an option goes beyond what the passage supports, reject it.

Vocabulary in Context

Vocabulary-in-context questions ask for the meaning of a word or expression as it is used in a particular passage. The correct answer is not necessarily the most common dictionary meaning of the word.

A word can have different meanings depending on its context. Therefore, read the sentence containing the word and examine the sentences before and after it.

How to Determine Meaning from Context

  1. Read the entire sentence containing the word or expression.
  2. Read the surrounding sentences for additional clues.
  3. Identify whether the word is used positively, negatively or neutrally.
  4. Replace the word mentally with each answer option.
  5. Select the option that preserves the meaning of the original sentence.

Context Clues

Context clues are pieces of information surrounding an unfamiliar word that help reveal its meaning. A writer may provide a definition, example, contrast or explanation near the word.

For example, in the sentence, The man's generosity was evident because he regularly donated food and clothing to poor families, the examples of donating food and clothing provide a clue to the meaning of generosity.

Reference Questions

Comprehension questions may ask what a pronoun or expression refers to. Words such as he, she, it, they, this, that, these and those usually refer to something mentioned earlier in the passage.

To answer a reference question, read the sentence containing the reference word and examine the preceding sentences. Then identify the noun or idea that agrees with the reference in both meaning and grammar.

Writer's Purpose

The writer's purpose is the reason the passage was written. Common purposes include informing, explaining, describing, persuading, criticizing, warning, advising, comparing or entertaining.

To identify the purpose, consider the overall effect of the passage rather than relying on one sentence. A passage that presents facts and explanations is likely to inform or explain, while a passage that attempts to convince readers to accept a particular position is likely to persuade.

Tone and Attitude

The tone of a passage is the writer's attitude towards the subject or people being discussed. The tone may be positive, negative, critical, sympathetic, humorous, serious, doubtful, approving, disapproving or neutral.

Words chosen by the writer often reveal the tone. For example, strongly negative words may indicate criticism or disapproval, while words expressing praise may indicate approval.

Cause and Effect

Some comprehension passages explain why something happened and what resulted from it. Words such as because, since, therefore, thus, consequently, as a result and so can signal cause-and-effect relationships.

When answering such questions, distinguish carefully between the cause and the effect. The cause is the reason something happens, while the effect is the result.

Contrast and Comparison

Writers often compare two ideas or contrast one idea with another. Signal words include however, although, but, yet, while, whereas, unlike and on the other hand.

These words are important because the writer may change direction after using them. Pay particular attention to statements following contrast markers.

Fact and Opinion

A fact is a statement that can be verified, while an opinion expresses a belief, judgment or personal view. A comprehension passage may contain both.

When a question asks what the passage establishes, distinguish between information directly supported by the passage and an opinion that merely sounds reasonable.

Efficient Reading Strategy

You do not need to memorize every sentence of a comprehension passage. Read actively and build a mental map of the passage.

  1. Read the passage once to understand its general subject.
  2. Identify the writer's central argument or message.
  3. Notice important transitions such as however, therefore, although and consequently.
  4. Identify examples, explanations and evidence supporting the main idea.
  5. When answering a specific question, return to the relevant part of the passage.
  6. For vocabulary questions, use context rather than relying on the first dictionary meaning that comes to mind.
  7. Check that your selected answer is supported by the passage.

Eliminating Wrong Options

JAMB-style multiple-choice questions may contain options that look attractive but are not supported by the passage. Elimination can help when the answer is not immediately obvious.

  1. Eliminate an option that contradicts the passage.
  2. Eliminate an option that introduces information not found or supported in the passage.
  3. Eliminate an option that is too broad when the passage makes a narrower claim.
  4. Eliminate an option that is too narrow when the question asks about the whole passage.
  5. Be suspicious of extreme claims unless the passage clearly supports them.

Worked Example

Passage: Many students believe that studying for several hours without interruption is the best way to prepare for an examination. However, research and classroom experience suggest that shorter periods of focused study, separated by brief breaks, can help learners maintain concentration. The effectiveness of this approach also depends on how actively students engage with the material.

Question: What is the main idea of the passage?

Explanation: The passage contrasts prolonged uninterrupted study with shorter focused study periods and adds that active engagement is important. Therefore, the best main idea should cover the effectiveness of focused study and active learning rather than mention only breaks.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Choosing an answer because it sounds generally true.
  • Using personal knowledge instead of evidence from the passage.
  • Choosing a minor detail as the main idea.
  • Assuming that the dictionary meaning of a word is automatically correct in context.
  • Ignoring contrast or cause-and-effect signal words.
  • Reading only the sentence containing the answer instead of considering the surrounding context.
  • Selecting an inference that is possible but not actually supported by the passage.

Exam Rules to Remember

  1. The passage is the authority for the answer.
  2. For main-idea questions, think about the whole passage.
  3. For inference questions, choose only conclusions supported by the evidence.
  4. For vocabulary questions, determine meaning from context.
  5. For reference questions, trace the pronoun or expression back to its correct antecedent.
  6. Pay close attention to words that signal contrast, cause, effect, comparison and conclusion.
  7. Do not allow personal opinions or outside knowledge to override what the passage says.

Self-Assessment

After studying this lesson, you should be able to identify the subject and main idea of a passage, distinguish main ideas from supporting details, make reasonable inferences, determine the meaning of words and expressions from context, identify references, recognize the writer's purpose and tone, and eliminate answer options that are not supported by the passage.

Quick Revision Summary

Main idea: The central point of the passage.

Supporting detail: Information that explains, illustrates or supports the main idea.

Inference: A logical conclusion supported by information in the passage.

Vocabulary in context: The meaning a word or expression has in the particular passage.

Reference: The person, thing or idea to which a pronoun or expression refers.

Writer's purpose: The reason the writer produced the passage.

Tone: The writer's attitude towards the subject or people discussed.

lessons.title: Grammatical Accuracy
lessons.html:
Grammatical Accuracy

Grammatical accuracy is the ability to use English words and sentences according to the accepted rules of grammar. In JAMB Use of English, questions on grammatical accuracy test your ability to identify and select expressions that are grammatically correct and appropriate in context.

This area commonly involves tense, aspect, number, concord, pronouns, question tags, modifiers, prepositions, conjunctions, and sentence structure. To answer these questions correctly, you must understand how words function together in a sentence rather than simply memorising isolated rules.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • distinguish between the major English tenses and use them correctly;
  • understand tense and aspect in relation to time and completed or continuing actions;
  • apply the rules of singular and plural number;
  • use subject-verb concord correctly;
  • identify common errors involving pronouns, prepositions and conjunctions;
  • form and answer question tags correctly;
  • identify grammatical errors in sentences; and
  • apply grammatical rules when answering objective questions.

1. Tense

Tense refers to the form of a verb that indicates the time of an action or state. English commonly expresses actions in the present, past and future.

Present Tense

The simple present is used for habits, routines, general truths and permanent situations.

  • She goes to school every day.
  • The earth moves round the sun.
  • Water boils at 100°C under standard atmospheric pressure.

With a third-person singular subject such as he, she or it, the main verb normally takes -s or -es.

Past Tense

The simple past expresses an action that occurred and was completed in the past.

  • They visited Lagos yesterday.
  • She finished the assignment last night.
  • The teacher entered the classroom five minutes ago.

Future Tense

The future is commonly expressed with will or other future constructions.

  • I will attend the meeting tomorrow.
  • They will complete the work soon.

2. Aspect

Aspect shows how an action relates to time, especially whether it is continuing, completed, or continuing up to a particular time. The major aspects useful in grammatical accuracy are the simple, progressive, perfect and perfect progressive forms.

Simple Aspect

The simple aspect presents an action as a fact, habit, completed event or general occurrence.

  • She reads every evening.
  • He visited Abuja last week.

Progressive Aspect

The progressive aspect shows an action that is in progress.

  • She is reading now.
  • They were playing when the rain started.

Perfect Aspect

The perfect aspect indicates that an action has been completed or occurred before another point in time.

  • She has finished her work.
  • They had left before we arrived.

Perfect Progressive Aspect

The perfect progressive combines completion or duration with an ongoing activity.

  • She has been studying for three hours.
  • They had been waiting for an hour before the bus arrived.

3. Sequence of Tenses

When two or more verbs occur in the same sentence, their tenses should normally agree logically with the time relationships between the actions.

  • When I arrived, the lecture had started.
  • She said that she was tired.
  • He will come when he finishes his work.

A common JAMB trap is to select a tense merely because it sounds familiar without considering the relationship between the actions.

4. The Use of Auxiliary Verbs

Auxiliary verbs such as be, have and do help to form tenses, questions, negatives and other grammatical structures.

  • She is reading.
  • They have arrived.
  • Do you understand?
  • He did not attend the meeting.

Remember that after did, the main verb must be in its base form.

  • Correct: She did go home.
  • Incorrect: She did went home.

5. Number

Number refers to whether a noun or pronoun is singular or plural. This distinction is important because it affects the form of the verb used with the subject.

  • The boy is here. (singular)
  • The boys are here. (plural)

Some nouns have irregular plural forms:

  • man → men
  • woman → women
  • child → children
  • mouse → mice
  • tooth → teeth

6. Concord or Subject-Verb Agreement

Concord is the grammatical agreement between words in a sentence. In grammatical accuracy questions, subject-verb agreement is particularly important.

A singular subject normally takes a singular verb, while a plural subject normally takes a plural verb in the present tense.

  • The student works hard.
  • The students work hard.
  • My brother is at home.
  • My brothers are at home.

Words Such as Each, Every, Either and Neither

Each, every, either and neither normally take singular verbs when they function as singular subjects.

  • Each of the candidates has a question paper.
  • Every student is expected to participate.
  • Neither of the boys was present.
  • Either of the answers is acceptable.

One of + Plural Noun

In a construction such as one of the students, the subject is one, not students. Therefore, the verb is singular.

  • One of the students is absent.
  • One of the books was missing.

Collective Nouns

Collective nouns such as team, committee, family and class can refer to a group as a single unit. The verb should agree with the intended meaning and the variety of English being used.

  • The committee has reached a decision.
  • The family is travelling tomorrow.

Subjects Joined by And

Two subjects joined by and normally take a plural verb.

  • John and Mary are friends.
  • The teacher and the students were in the hall.

However, when two nouns refer to one person, thing or idea, a singular verb may be appropriate.

  • The owner and manager is here.

Subjects Joined by Either...or and Neither...nor

With either...or and neither...nor, the verb generally agrees with the subject nearer to it.

  • Either the teacher or the students are responsible.
  • Either the students or the teacher is responsible.
  • Neither the boys nor the girl was present.
  • Neither the girl nor the boys were present.

7. Pronoun Agreement

A pronoun should agree with the noun it refers to in number and, where relevant, person and gender.

  • Each candidate must bring his or her identification slip.
  • The students submitted their assignments.
  • The woman said that she was ready.

Be careful not to create disagreement between a pronoun and its antecedent.

8. Relative Pronouns

Relative pronouns introduce clauses that give additional information about a noun.

  • Who is generally used for people.
  • Which is generally used for things and animals.
  • That can be used for people, animals and things in many defining relative clauses.
  • Whose expresses possession.
  • The man who spoke to me is a doctor.
  • The book which I bought is interesting.
  • The student whose bag was missing reported the matter.

9. Prepositions

Prepositions show relationships involving time, place, direction, position or other connections.

Common examples include in, on, at, by, with, from, to, for and between.

  • He arrived at the station early.
  • She lives in Lagos.
  • The examination begins at 8:00 a.m.
  • The book is on the table.

Some verbs and adjectives are conventionally followed by particular prepositions. These combinations should be learnt as units.

  • depend on
  • insist on
  • belong to
  • interested in
  • good at
  • afraid of

10. Conjunctions

Conjunctions join words, phrases or clauses. Common conjunctions include and, but, or, because, although, unless, while and if.

  • She studied hard because she wanted to pass.
  • He is poor but honest.
  • Although it rained, the match continued.

Avoid using two conjunctions where only one is required.

  • Correct: Although he was tired, he continued working.
  • Incorrect: Although he was tired, but he continued working.

11. Modifiers

A modifier is a word, phrase or clause that gives more information about another part of a sentence. A modifier should be placed close enough to the word it modifies to avoid confusion.

  • Correct: She carefully answered the question.
  • Incorrect or unclear: She answered the question careful.

Pay special attention to misplaced modifiers in examination questions because they can make an otherwise familiar sentence grammatically or logically faulty.

12. Question Tags

A question tag is a short question added to the end of a statement. It is commonly used to seek confirmation.

A positive statement normally takes a negative tag, while a negative statement normally takes a positive tag.

  • You are coming, aren't you?
  • She is not ready, is she?
  • They have arrived, haven't they?
  • He does not know, does he?

Using the Correct Auxiliary

The auxiliary in the question tag normally corresponds to the auxiliary in the statement.

  • She is happy, isn't she?
  • They have finished, haven't they?
  • You can swim, can't you?

When there is no auxiliary in the statement, use the appropriate form of do, does or did.

  • He plays football, doesn't he?
  • They went home, didn't they?

Special Case: I am

The usual question tag for a positive statement beginning with I am is aren't I?

  • I am late, aren't I?

Imperatives and Requests

Commands and requests can take special tags, often involving will you?, won't you? or shall we?, depending on the intended meaning.

  • Open the door, will you?
  • Let's go, shall we?

13. Common Grammatical Errors

The following errors frequently occur in formal English:

  • Wrong: He does not knows the answer. Correct: He does not know the answer.
  • Wrong: She did went home. Correct: She did go home.
  • Wrong: Each of the boys have a book. Correct: Each of the boys has a book.
  • Wrong: One of my friends are here. Correct: One of my friends is here.
  • Wrong: Neither of the answers are correct. Correct: Neither of the answers is correct.
  • Wrong: Although he was tired, but he continued. Correct: Although he was tired, he continued.

14. How to Approach JAMB Grammatical Accuracy Questions

When you encounter a grammatical accuracy question, do not select an option merely because it sounds familiar. Apply a systematic process.

  1. Read the entire sentence. Do not focus only on the blank.
  2. Identify the subject. Determine whether it is singular or plural.
  3. Identify the verb and its time reference. Check whether the tense and aspect fit the meaning.
  4. Check concord. Make sure the subject and verb agree.
  5. Check pronouns. Ensure that pronouns agree with their antecedents.
  6. Check prepositions and conjunctions. Make sure the construction is idiomatic and logical.
  7. Check the complete sentence. The correct option must produce a grammatical and meaningful sentence.

15. Worked Examples

Example 1

Question: Each of the candidates _____ expected to arrive early.

  • A. are
  • B. were
  • C. is
  • D. have

Answer: C. is

Explanation: The subject is each, which is singular. Therefore, the singular verb is is required.

Example 2

Question: If she _____ earlier, she would have met the principal.

  • A. arrived
  • B. had arrived
  • C. arrives
  • D. has arrived

Answer: B. had arrived

Explanation: The sentence expresses an unreal condition in the past. The if-clause therefore uses the past perfect: had arrived.

Example 3

Question: The students did not _____ the instruction.

  • A. understood
  • B. understanding
  • C. understand
  • D. understands

Answer: C. understand

Explanation: After the auxiliary did, the main verb takes its base form.

Example 4

Question: Musa is a hardworking student, _____?

  • A. is he
  • B. isn't he
  • C. doesn't he
  • D. wasn't he

Answer: B. isn't he

Explanation: The statement is positive and contains the auxiliary is. Therefore, the tag is negative: isn't he?

16. Examination Traps to Watch For

  • Ignore intervening nouns. In “The quality of the products is good,” the subject is quality, not products.
  • Do not confuse tense with time expressions. Always consider the relationship between actions.
  • Watch auxiliary verbs. After does or did, use the base form of the main verb.
  • Do not let a nearby plural noun control the verb. Identify the real subject first.
  • Check the whole expression. An option may contain a grammatically correct word but produce an incorrect sentence in context.
  • Pay attention to negative words. Words such as not, never, hardly and rarely can affect the grammatical structure.

17. Quick Revision Rules

  • Singular subjects normally take singular verbs in the simple present.
  • Plural subjects normally take plural verbs in the simple present.
  • Each, every, either and neither normally take singular verbs.
  • In one of + plural noun, the verb agrees with one.
  • After did, use the base form of the verb.
  • After does, use the base form of the verb.
  • A positive statement normally takes a negative question tag.
  • A negative statement normally takes a positive question tag.
  • Use the auxiliary of the statement when forming a question tag.
  • Two subjects joined by and normally take a plural verb.
  • With either...or and neither...nor, the verb generally agrees with the nearer subject.
  • Pronouns must agree appropriately with the nouns they refer to.
  • Prepositions should be used according to standard English usage and established word combinations.

18. Self-Assessment

Before leaving this lesson, test yourself without looking back at the explanations.

  1. Neither of the boys _____ present. (was/were)
  2. She did not _____ the message. (receive/received)
  3. One of the teachers _____ absent. (is/are)
  4. They have completed the work, _____? (haven't they/have they)
  5. Each student _____ a locker. (has/have)
  6. If he had studied harder, he _____ the examination. (would have passed/will pass)

Answers: 1. was; 2. receive; 3. is; 4. haven't they; 5. has; 6. would have passed.

Conclusion

Grammatical accuracy requires more than memorising individual rules. You must learn to identify the subject, understand the time relationship between actions, recognise the function of auxiliary verbs, and examine how different parts of a sentence relate to one another. Regular practice with objective questions will help you recognise grammatical patterns quickly.

For JAMB preparation, use the official syllabus as your scope of study and practise applying each grammatical rule in context. The aim is not merely to know that a rule exists, but to recognise the correct construction quickly and accurately when faced with four answer options.
