lessons.title: Homonyms and Homophones
lessons.html:
Homonyms and Homophones

Homonyms and homophones are words that can easily confuse candidates because they may have the same pronunciation, the same spelling, or both, while having different meanings. In JAMB Use of English, understanding these relationships helps you choose the word that correctly completes a sentence and distinguish words that sound alike.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • Define homonyms and homophones.
  • Distinguish between homonyms, homophones, and related word forms.
  • Identify the correct word from context.
  • Use common homonym and homophone pairs correctly in sentences.
  • Avoid common spelling and word-choice errors in examination questions.

What Are Homonyms?

Homonyms are words that have the same spelling or the same pronunciation but have different meanings. The word homonym is therefore a broad term for words that share an important aspect of their form but differ in meaning.

For example:

  • bank can mean a financial institution: I deposited money in the bank.
  • bank can also mean the side of a river: The children sat on the river bank.

The spelling and pronunciation of bank remain the same, but its meaning changes according to the context.

Types of Homonyms

Homonyms are commonly discussed in two useful groups: homographs and homophones.

Homographs

Homographs are words that have the same spelling but different meanings. Some homographs are pronounced differently, while others may have the same pronunciation.

Examples include:

  • lead – to guide: The teacher will lead the students.
  • lead – a type of metal: The pipe contains lead.
  • tear – a drop from the eye: A tear rolled down her cheek.
  • tear – to pull apart: Do not tear the paper.

In examination questions, the sentence usually provides enough context to determine the intended meaning and, where necessary, pronunciation.

What Are Homophones?

Homophones are words that have the same or very similar pronunciation but different spellings and meanings.

For example, principal and principle sound alike in standard English, but they do not mean the same thing.

  • principal – the head of a school or the most important person or thing: The principal addressed the students.
  • principle – a fundamental rule, belief, or standard: Honesty is an important principle.

Because the words sound alike, you must use the meaning of the sentence to select the correct spelling.

Common Homophones You Should Know

WordMeaningExample
acceptto receive or agree to somethingShe accepted the invitation.
exceptexcluding or leaving outEveryone came except Musa.
advicean opinion or recommendationHe gave me useful advice.
adviseto recommend or counselI advise you to study regularly.
aislea passage between rows of seats or shelvesShe walked down the aisle.
islean islandThey visited a beautiful isle.
altara raised place used in religious ceremoniesThe couple stood before the altar.
alterto change somethingDo not alter the document.
bareuncovered or without clothingHe walked on the bare floor.
bearan animal; also to tolerate or carryI cannot bear the noise.
brakea device for stopping or slowing a vehiclePress the brake carefully.
breakto separate, damage, or interruptBe careful not to break the glass.
citeto quote or refer to a sourceThe writer cited several examples.
sightthe ability to see or something seenThe mountain was a beautiful sight.
sitea place or locationThey selected a site for the building.
complementsomething that completes or enhances another thingThe shoes complement her dress.
complimentan expression of praiseShe received a compliment.
dearbeloved or expensiveShe is a dear friend.
deera hoofed animalWe saw a deer in the forest.
farethe price paid for a journeyThe bus fare has increased.
fairjust, reasonable, or an exhibitionThe judge gave a fair decision.
flourpowder made from grain and used in cookingShe bought flour for the cake.
flowerthe blossom of a plantThe flower smells pleasant.
hearto perceive soundCan you hear me?
herein or at this placeCome here.
knighta medieval soldierThe knight rode a horse.
nightthe period of darknessWe arrived at night.
knowto have knowledgeI know the answer.
noa negative responseNo, I do not agree.
principalhead of a school; most importantThe principal spoke to us.
principlea basic rule or beliefHe acted according to his principles.
stationarynot movingThe vehicle remained stationary.
stationerywriting materialsI bought stationery for school.
theirbelonging to themThe students submitted their books.
therein or at that placePut the bag there.
they'recontraction of they areThey're coming soon.
weatherthe condition of the atmosphereThe weather is pleasant.
whetherused when expressing alternatives or uncertaintyI do not know whether he will come.
yourbelonging to youWhere is your book?
you'recontraction of you areYou're doing well.

Important Pairs Commonly Confused in Examinations

Principal and Principle

Principal refers to a person who is in charge of a school or something that is first in importance. Principle refers to a rule, belief, or fundamental truth.

The school principal addressed the assembly.

She refuses to compromise her principles.

Stationary and Stationery

Stationary means remaining still, while stationery means writing materials such as paper, envelopes, and pens.

The bus remained stationary.

The secretary ordered new stationery.

Advice and Advise

Advice is a noun meaning a recommendation or guidance. Advise is a verb meaning to give advice.

My father gave me good advice.

My father advised me to work harder.

Complement and Compliment

Complement refers to something that completes or improves another thing. Compliment means praise or an expression of admiration.

The red shoes complement her outfit.

The teacher complimented the student on her performance.

Accept and Except

Accept means to receive, agree to, or approve something. Except means excluding someone or something.

He accepted the offer.

All the candidates passed except one.

Homophones in Oral Forms

JAMB also tests oral English features, including rhymes and homophones. In this area, attention is given to words that have the same pronunciation but different meanings and spellings.

For example, sea and see have the same pronunciation but different meanings:

  • sea – a large body of salt water: The ship crossed the sea.
  • see – to perceive with the eyes: I can see the building.

In an oral-form question, listen carefully to the sound and then consider the meaning and spelling required by the sentence.

How to Answer Homonym and Homophone Questions

When faced with a question involving confusing words, do not choose an option simply because it sounds correct. Follow these steps:

  1. Read the complete sentence. The surrounding words often reveal the intended meaning.
  2. Identify the grammatical function. Determine whether the missing word should be a noun, verb, adjective, adverb, or another word class.
  3. Determine the meaning required. Ask what idea the sentence is communicating.
  4. Compare the options carefully. If two options sound alike, check their spellings and meanings.
  5. Insert the option into the sentence. Read the sentence again to confirm that the meaning and grammar are correct.

Context Is the Key

The most important skill in solving these questions is understanding context. A word may sound exactly like another word, but only one spelling may make sense in the sentence.

Consider this example:

The school bought new ______ for the examination hall.

The correct answer is stationery because the sentence refers to writing materials. Stationary means not moving and would not fit the context.

Common Examination Traps

  • Sounding alike does not mean meaning alike. Do not select a word simply because it has the expected pronunciation.
  • Watch the spelling. A single letter can completely change the meaning of a word.
  • Check the part of speech. Words such as advice and advise differ not only in spelling but also in grammatical function.
  • Do not confuse contractions with ordinary words. You're means you are, while your shows possession.
  • Use the entire sentence. Looking only at the word immediately before the blank may lead to the wrong answer.

Worked Examples

Example 1

Question: The school ______ addressed the students during assembly.

Answer: principal

Explanation: The sentence refers to the head of a school. Therefore, principal is correct, not principle.

Example 2

Question: The driver applied the ______ when the child crossed the road.

Answer: brake

Explanation: A brake is used to slow or stop a vehicle. Break means to damage, separate, or interrupt something.

Example 3

Question: All the candidates were present ______ Musa.

Answer: except

Explanation: The sentence excludes Musa from the group, so except is required. Accept means to receive or agree to something.

Example 4

Question: The teacher gave the students useful ______ before the examination.

Answer: advice

Explanation: The blank requires a noun because it refers to guidance given by the teacher. Advice is the noun, while advise is the verb.

Quick Comparison

TermKey FeatureExample
HomonymWords share spelling or pronunciation but have different meanings.bank – financial institution / side of a river
HomographWords have the same spelling but different meanings.lead – guide / metal
HomophoneWords have the same pronunciation but different spellings and meanings.sea / see

Self-Test

Choose the word that correctly completes each sentence.

  1. The school ______ gave a speech during assembly. (principal / principle)
  2. Honesty is an important ______ of good character. (principal / principle)
  3. The car remained ______ while the driver waited. (stationary / stationery)
  4. She bought some writing ______ from the shop. (stationary / stationery)
  5. The doctor gave him useful ______. (advice / advise)
  6. I would ______ you to revise your notes. (advice / advise)
  7. Everyone attended the meeting ______ the chairman. (accept / except)
  8. She decided to ______ the invitation. (accept / except)
  9. The students walked down the ______ between the seats. (aisle / isle)
  10. The holiday resort is located on a small ______. (aisle / isle)

Answers to the Self-Test

  1. principal – the head of a school.
  2. principle – a basic rule or belief.
  3. stationary – not moving.
  4. stationery – writing materials.
  5. advice – guidance or recommendation; a noun.
  6. advise – to give guidance; a verb.
  7. except – excluding.
  8. accept – to receive or agree to something.
  9. aisle – a passage between rows of seats or shelves.
  10. isle – an island.

JAMB Examination Strategy

JAMB's Use of English syllabus expects candidates to identify and interpret words in context and to distinguish relevant oral forms, including homophones. Therefore, do not attempt to memorise isolated spellings alone. Learn the meaning, grammatical function, spelling, and usage of commonly confused words.

A useful revision method is to create pairs in your notes and write one sentence for each word. For example, write principal and principle together, then construct a sentence that clearly demonstrates the meaning of each. This makes it easier to recall the correct word under examination conditions.

Key Points to Remember

  • Homonyms involve words that share spelling or pronunciation but have different meanings.
  • Homophones sound alike but differ in spelling and meaning.
  • Homographs have the same spelling but different meanings.
  • Context is the strongest clue when choosing between confusing words.
  • Pay attention to both meaning and grammatical function.
  • Practise common pairs such as principal/principle, stationary/stationery, advice/advise, accept/except, and complement/compliment.
  • For oral-form questions, listen for the sound but use the sentence context to determine the appropriate word.

Final Revision Summary

Homonyms and homophones test your ability to recognise differences in meaning, spelling, and usage. Two words may sound alike but require completely different spellings, while words with identical spelling may have different meanings or pronunciations. In a JAMB question, the correct answer is determined by the meaning and grammatical requirements of the sentence. Always read the whole sentence, identify the intended meaning, check the part of speech, and then select the word whose spelling and usage fit the context.

lessons.title: Idioms
lessons.html:
Idioms

Idioms are an important part of English vocabulary and are tested under Lexis and Structure in the JAMB Use of English syllabus. JAMB specifically states that candidates should be tested on ordinary usage, figurative usage and idiomatic usage, and that the idioms tested should be formal and expressed in standard British English.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • define an idiom and distinguish it from ordinary and figurative expressions;
  • recognise common idiomatic expressions used in standard British English;
  • explain the meanings of idioms from context;
  • select the correct idiom to complete a sentence;
  • distinguish between idioms with similar or related meanings;
  • avoid interpreting idioms literally when their context gives them a figurative meaning.

1. What Is an Idiom?

An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning is different from, or cannot always be understood simply by adding together, the literal meanings of the individual words.

For example, in the sentence “The examination was a piece of cake,” the expression “a piece of cake” does not refer to food. It means that the examination was very easy.

Idioms are usually learned as complete expressions. Changing the words carelessly may destroy the intended meaning or make the expression grammatically incorrect.

2. Ordinary, Figurative and Idiomatic Usage

Ordinary Usage

In ordinary usage, words generally have their direct or literal meanings.

Example: The boy broke the window.

Here, broke means physically damaged or shattered something.

Figurative Usage

Figurative usage gives a word or expression a meaning that goes beyond its literal meaning, often to create an image or comparison.

Example: The news broke his heart.

The expression does not mean that his physical heart was broken. It means that he was deeply saddened.

Idiomatic Usage

Idiomatic usage involves a conventional expression whose established meaning may not be predictable from the individual words.

Example: The new manager is pulling the strings.

This does not mean that the manager is physically pulling strings. It means that the manager is secretly controlling or influencing events.

3. Characteristics of Idioms

Idioms commonly have the following characteristics:

  • They have an established meaning: Their meaning is generally recognised by proficient users of the language.
  • They are relatively fixed: The words and grammatical pattern usually cannot be changed freely.
  • The meaning may not be literal: The expression often communicates an idea different from its individual words.
  • Context is important: The surrounding sentence can help you determine the intended meaning.
  • They can perform different grammatical functions: Some function as verbs, some as noun phrases, adjectives or adverbial expressions.

4. Common JAMB-Level Idioms and Their Meanings

The following formal idiomatic expressions are useful for examination preparation. Learn both the expression and the meaning, then practise identifying the meaning from context.

Expressions Relating to Difficulty and Ease

  • A piece of cake — something very easy.
  • Take the bull by the horns — confront a difficult situation boldly and directly.
  • Have one's hands full — be very busy or have a lot to deal with.
  • Be in deep water — be in serious difficulty or trouble.
  • Be in a tight corner — be in a difficult or embarrassing situation.

Expressions Relating to Success and Failure

  • Hit the nail on the head — describe something exactly or identify the main point correctly.
  • Come off with flying colours — succeed very well.
  • Miss the boat — lose an opportunity.
  • Go to the dogs — deteriorate or become worse.
  • Throw in the towel — give up or admit defeat.

Expressions Relating to Knowledge and Understanding

  • Get the hang of something — learn how to do something or begin to understand it.
  • Be in the dark — be unaware or uninformed about something.
  • Know the ropes — know how a particular system or activity works.
  • Read between the lines — look for or understand a hidden or implied meaning.
  • See eye to eye — agree completely with someone.

Expressions Relating to Secrecy and Information

  • Let the cat out of the bag — reveal a secret, usually unintentionally.
  • Spill the beans — reveal secret information.
  • Keep something under one's hat — keep something secret.
  • Give the game away — reveal a secret or disclose an advantage.

Expressions Relating to People and Behaviour

  • Pull someone's leg — tease or joke with someone.
  • Put one's foot in one's mouth — say something embarrassing or inappropriate.
  • Lose one's temper — become angry.
  • Keep one's cool — remain calm.
  • Get on someone's nerves — annoy or irritate someone.
  • See red — become extremely angry.

Expressions Relating to Money

  • Make ends meet — have enough money to cover one's necessary expenses.
  • Cost an arm and a leg — be extremely expensive.
  • Live beyond one's means — spend more money than one can afford.
  • Bring home the bacon — earn money to support oneself or one's family.

Expressions Relating to Decisions and Actions

  • Make up one's mind — make a decision.
  • Take the plunge — make an important or decisive move after hesitation.
  • Jump to conclusions — reach a judgement without having enough evidence.
  • Take something into account — consider something when making a decision.
  • Put one's foot down — refuse firmly to accept something or insist on a particular course of action.

5. Idioms in Context

In JAMB questions, you should not depend only on memorisation. The meaning of an idiom is often tested through a sentence. Read the entire sentence before selecting an answer.

Example: When the principal discovered the students' plan, he decided to take the bull by the horns.

Meaning: He decided to confront the situation boldly and directly.

Example: Ada was completely in the dark about the changes to the examination timetable.

Meaning: Ada was unaware of the changes.

Example: The new computer system cost the company an arm and a leg.

Meaning: The computer system was extremely expensive.

6. How to Answer Idiom Questions

Step 1: Read the Whole Sentence

Do not select an answer merely because one option looks familiar. Read the complete sentence and identify what is happening.

Step 2: Identify the Idiomatic Expression

Look for a group of words that appears to have a meaning beyond its literal interpretation.

Step 3: Replace the Idiom With a Simple Meaning

Mentally substitute the likely meaning of the idiom into the sentence. Ask yourself whether the sentence still makes logical sense.

Step 4: Check the Context

The surrounding words should support the meaning you have chosen. Context is especially important when two idioms have similar meanings.

Step 5: Check Grammar

An idiom must fit grammatically into the sentence. Pay attention to tense, subject, number and the words that normally occur with the expression.

7. Commonly Confused Idioms and Expressions

Make Ends Meet vs. Live Beyond One's Means

Make ends meet means to have enough money to pay for basic needs.

Live beyond one's means means to spend more money than one can afford.

Example: Although Musa earns a modest salary, he manages to make ends meet.

See Eye to Eye vs. See Red

See eye to eye means to agree with someone.

See red means to become extremely angry.

Give the Game Away vs. Let the Cat Out of the Bag

Both expressions can mean to reveal information that was supposed to remain secret. The exact choice depends on the context and grammatical structure of the sentence.

Throw in the Towel vs. Take the Plunge

Throw in the towel means to give up.

Take the plunge means to make a decisive move, especially after hesitation.

8. Literal Meaning Versus Idiomatic Meaning

A major source of difficulty is the tendency to interpret an idiom literally. In examination questions, this can lead to choosing an incorrect option.

Example: “The chairman put his foot down.”

The expression does not necessarily mean that the chairman physically placed his foot on the ground. In an appropriate context, it means that he refused firmly to change his decision or accept something.

Always ask: Does the literal meaning make sense in this context? If it does not, look for the established idiomatic meaning.

9. Idioms and Standard British English

JAMB states that the idioms tested should be formal and expressed in standard British English. Therefore, candidates should concentrate on established English expressions and their accepted meanings rather than informal slang or expressions whose usage is uncertain.

Remember that an idiom may have a particular grammatical form. For example, make ends meet is normally used as a complete expression; changing it unnecessarily may make the sentence incorrect.

10. Worked Examples

Example 1

Question: The manager told the workers to stop wasting time and get their act together.

A. start quarrelling
A. leave the workplace
A. organise themselves and improve their performance
A. change their uniforms

Answer: Organise themselves and improve their performance.

Explanation: Get one's act together means to become organised and start behaving or performing more effectively.

Example 2

Question: The witness's statement threw light on the mysterious incident.

A. made the incident more confusing
A. helped to explain the incident
A. caused the incident
A. prevented an investigation

Answer: Helped to explain the incident.

Explanation: Throw light on something means to provide information that helps explain or clarify it.

Example 3

Question: After several unsuccessful attempts, the candidate decided to throw in the towel.

A. continue trying
A. give up
A. celebrate
A. ask for assistance

Answer: Give up.

Explanation: Throw in the towel means to stop trying because one accepts defeat.

11. Practice Exercise

Choose the option that best explains the meaning of the underlined expression in each sentence.

1. The principal decided to put his foot down over the students' repeated lateness.

A. punish himself
B. take a firm stand
C. walk away
D. become confused

2. The young businessman has finally made ends meet.

A. become extremely rich
B. earned enough to cover his necessary expenses
C. borrowed a large sum of money
D. stopped working

3. Do not jump to conclusions before hearing both sides of the story.

A. reach a judgement too quickly
B. avoid making a decision
C. change the subject
D. ask an unnecessary question

4. The secretary accidentally let the cat out of the bag.

A. lost an animal
B. caused confusion
C. revealed a secret
D. escaped from the office

5. The students came off with flying colours in the examination.

A. performed very successfully
B. arrived late
C. failed completely
D. changed their examination centre

12. Answers to the Practice Exercise

  1. B — take a firm stand. Put one's foot down means to insist firmly on something or refuse to accept something.
  2. B — earned enough to cover his necessary expenses. Make ends meet means to have enough money for one's basic needs.
  3. A — reach a judgement too quickly. Jump to conclusions means to form an opinion without sufficient evidence.
  4. C — revealed a secret. Let the cat out of the bag means to disclose secret information.
  5. A — performed very successfully. Come off with flying colours means to succeed very well.

13. Examination Tips

  • Learn idioms together with their meanings, not as isolated words.
  • Pay close attention to the context of the sentence.
  • Do not automatically choose the literal meaning of an expression.
  • Watch for grammatical clues around the idiom.
  • Distinguish between expressions that mean similar things by considering the context.
  • Give preference to established standard English expressions rather than slang.
  • Practise using idioms in sentences so that their meanings become easier to recognise.
  • When unsure, eliminate options that do not fit the meaning or grammar of the sentence.

14. Quick Revision Table

IdiomMeaning
A piece of cakeSomething very easy
Take the bull by the hornsConfront a difficult situation boldly
In deep waterIn serious trouble
Hit the nail on the headIdentify or describe something exactly
Come off with flying coloursSucceed very well
Miss the boatLose an opportunity
Throw in the towelGive up
Be in the darkBe unaware or uninformed
See eye to eyeAgree completely
Let the cat out of the bagReveal a secret
Pull someone's legTease or joke with someone
Keep one's coolRemain calm
Make ends meetHave enough money for necessary expenses
Cost an arm and a legBe extremely expensive
Jump to conclusionsJudge too quickly without sufficient evidence
Put one's foot downTake a firm stand

15. Final Summary

An idiom is a fixed expression whose established meaning is not always the same as the literal meaning of its individual words. For JAMB Use of English, candidates should understand the difference between ordinary, figurative and idiomatic usage and be able to interpret expressions within sentences. Since JAMB specifies that the idioms tested should be formal and expressed in standard British English, preparation should focus on recognised standard expressions and their meanings in context.

Key rule: Do not ask only, “What do these words mean literally?” Ask, “What does this complete expression mean in this sentence?”

Self-Check

Before leaving this lesson, make sure you can explain the meaning of at least ten idioms without looking at your notes, distinguish an idiom from a literal expression, and correctly interpret an idiom from its context. If you cannot, revise the examples and practise using each expression in a new sentence.

lessons.title: Lexis and Structure
lessons.html:
Lexis and Structure

Lexis and Structure is a major area of JAMB Use of English. It tests a candidate's knowledge of vocabulary, grammatical structures, sentence relationships, correct usage, punctuation, spelling, and the meanings of words and expressions in different contexts. According to the JAMB Use of English syllabus, candidates are expected to identify words and expressions in ordinary, figurative and idiomatic contexts, determine similar and opposite meanings, recognise correct grammatical patterns, distinguish correct from incorrect punctuation and spelling, and interpret information conveyed in sentences.

1. Synonyms

A synonym is a word or expression that has the same or nearly the same meaning as another word or expression. In JAMB questions, the meaning required is usually determined by the context in which the word is used.

For example, abundant means plentiful, while rapid means swift or fast.

However, synonyms are not always interchangeable in every sentence. A word may have several meanings, so always consider the context before selecting an answer.

Examples

  • Brief — short
  • Commence — begin
  • Diligent — hardworking
  • Hostile — unfriendly
  • Obtain — acquire
  • Reluctant — unwilling
  • Transparent — clear
  • Vast — enormous

JAMB tip: Do not choose an option simply because it looks similar to the given word. Replace the word mentally in the sentence and check which option preserves the original meaning.

2. Antonyms

An antonym is a word that has an opposite or contrasting meaning to another word. JAMB may ask you to select the word that is opposite in meaning to a given word as it is used in a sentence.

Examples

  • Ancient — modern
  • Artificial — natural
  • Expand — contract
  • Generous — stingy
  • Permanent — temporary
  • Permit — forbid
  • Rigid — flexible
  • Victory — defeat

Some words have different opposites depending on context. For example, light may be opposed to heavy when referring to weight, but to dark when referring to brightness.

JAMB tip: Read the complete sentence before deciding what the opposite meaning should be.

3. Homonyms

Homonyms are words that have the same form or pronunciation but different meanings. They can create difficulty because the correct interpretation depends on context.

Common examples

  • Bank — a financial institution; the side of a river.
  • Bark — the outer covering of a tree; the sound made by a dog.
  • Bat — a flying mammal; an implement used in some sports.
  • Light — illumination; something that is not heavy.
  • Match — a contest; a small stick used to produce fire.
  • Watch — to observe; a timepiece.

Homophones are words that sound alike but have different spellings and meanings, such as principal/principle, stationary/stationery, and compliment/complement.

Important distinctions

  • Principal means a chief person or something most important; principle means a fundamental rule or belief.
  • Stationary means not moving; stationery refers to writing materials.
  • Compliment means praise; complement means something that completes or enhances another thing.

4. Clauses

A clause is a group of words containing a subject and a finite verb. Clauses may be independent or dependent.

Independent clause

An independent clause expresses a complete thought and can stand as a sentence.

Example: The students arrived early.

Dependent clause

A dependent clause cannot normally stand alone as a complete sentence. It depends on another clause for its complete meaning.

Example: because the examination had started

In the sentence The students arrived early because the examination had started, the first clause is independent while the second is dependent.

Major types of dependent clauses

  • Noun clause: functions as a noun. Example: What he said was surprising.
  • Adjectival or relative clause: describes a noun or pronoun. Example: The student who won the prize is my friend.
  • Adverbial clause: performs the function of an adverb. Example: We left when the rain stopped.

5. Sentence Patterns

Sentence patterns describe the way the major elements of a sentence are arranged. The basic elements include the subject, verb, object, complement and adverbial.

Subject + Verb (SV)

Example: The baby cried.

Subject + Verb + Object (SVO)

Example: Ada opened the door.

Subject + Verb + Complement (SVC)

Example: The soup is delicious.

Subject + Verb + Indirect Object + Direct Object (SVOO)

Example: The teacher gave the students homework.

Subject + Verb + Object + Complement (SVOC)

Example: The committee elected Musa chairman.

JAMB tip: Identify the subject and the main verb first. Then determine what receives the action or completes the meaning of the verb.

6. Word Classes and Their Functions

Word classes describe groups of words according to their grammatical functions. A word can sometimes belong to different classes depending on how it is used in a sentence.

Nouns

Nouns name people, places, things, animals, qualities, states or ideas.

Examples: teacher, Lagos, book, honesty, freedom.

Pronouns

Pronouns are used in place of nouns or noun phrases.

Examples: he, she, it, they, we, who, which, someone.

Verbs

Verbs express actions, occurrences or states.

Examples: run, write, become, seem, know.

Adjectives

Adjectives describe or modify nouns and pronouns.

Example: The careful student answered correctly.

Adverbs

Adverbs can modify verbs, adjectives, other adverbs or entire clauses.

Example: She answered carefully.

Prepositions

Prepositions show relationships involving place, time, direction, possession or other connections.

Examples: in, on, at, under, between, beside, through, during.

Conjunctions

Conjunctions connect words, phrases or clauses.

Examples: and, but, or, because, although, while.

Determiners

Determiners occur before nouns and help identify or quantify them.

Examples: a, an, the, this, that, some, many, each.

Interjections

Interjections express sudden feelings or reactions.

Examples: Oh! Ah! Hurray! Alas!

Important: In JAMB questions, do not identify a word class from the word alone. Examine how the word functions in the particular sentence.

7. Mood

Grammatical mood indicates the attitude or purpose expressed by a verb construction.

Indicative mood

The indicative mood is used mainly to state facts, opinions or information.

Example: She lives in Abuja.

Imperative mood

The imperative mood is used for commands, instructions, requests or advice.

Examples: Close the door. Please listen carefully.

Subjunctive mood

The subjunctive is used in certain formal constructions involving wishes, demands, recommendations, hypothetical situations and requirements.

Example: It is important that every candidate be present.

8. Tense

Tense indicates the time relationship of an action or state. In standard English, the main tense distinctions are present and past, with future time commonly expressed through auxiliary constructions.

Simple present

Used for habits, general truths, repeated actions and states.

Example: She reads every evening.

Simple past

Used for completed actions in the past.

Example: She read the book yesterday.

Present continuous

Used for actions happening around the time of speaking or for temporary situations.

Example: She is reading now.

Past continuous

Used for an action that was in progress at a particular time in the past.

Example: She was reading when I arrived.

Present perfect

Used for past actions that have a present connection or for experiences up to the present.

Example: She has finished her work.

Past perfect

Used for an action completed before another past action.

Example: She had left before I arrived.

9. Aspect

Aspect shows how an action or situation extends through time. The common aspects tested in English include simple, progressive, perfect and perfect progressive constructions.

  • Simple: They play football.
  • Progressive: They are playing football.
  • Perfect: They have played football.
  • Perfect progressive: They have been playing football.

The progressive aspect commonly presents an action as ongoing, while the perfect aspect relates an earlier action or state to a later point in time.

10. Number

Number refers to whether a noun or pronoun is singular or plural.

  • Singular: book, child, woman, student.
  • Plural: books, children, women, students.

Some nouns have irregular plural forms. Examples include man/men, child/children, tooth/teeth, and criterion/criteria.

Some nouns that refer to groups may create agreement difficulties. The correct verb depends on whether the noun is being treated as a singular unit or as individual members in the context.

11. Agreement and Concord

Agreement, also called concord, means that related grammatical elements must correspond correctly in number, person or grammatical form.

Subject-verb agreement

A singular subject normally takes a singular verb in the present tense, while a plural subject takes a plural verb.

Correct: The boy plays football.

Correct: The boys play football.

Common concord traps

  • Each of the students is ready. The subject is each, not students.
  • Neither of the answers is correct.
  • The quality of the products is excellent. The head noun is quality.
  • One of the boys has arrived. The subject is one.
  • The news is encouraging. News is treated as singular.

Pay particular attention to expressions such as each of, every, neither of, either of, one of, and phrases beginning with the quality of or the number of.

12. Degrees of Comparison

Adjectives can express different degrees of comparison.

Positive degree

The basic form of the adjective is used without comparison.

Example: Tunde is tall.

Comparative degree

The comparative form is used when comparing two people or things.

Example: Tunde is taller than Musa.

Superlative degree

The superlative form is used when comparing one member with a group of three or more.

Example: Tunde is the tallest student in the class.

Irregular forms

  • Good — better — best
  • Bad — worse — worst
  • Little — less — least
  • Many/much — more — most
  • Far — farther/further — farthest/furthest

Avoid double comparison such as more better or most fastest.

13. Question Tags

A question tag is a short question added to a statement, usually to seek confirmation.

Positive statements normally take negative tags, while negative statements normally take positive tags.

  • She is coming, isn't she?
  • They arrived early, didn't they?
  • He does not smoke, does he?
  • You can swim, can't you?

The auxiliary verb in the statement is normally repeated in the tag. If there is no auxiliary, an appropriate form of do, does or did is used.

Special example: I am late, aren't I?

14. Punctuation and Mechanics

Punctuation marks help communicate the intended structure and meaning of written English. JAMB may test whether punctuation has been correctly used.

  • Full stop (.) ends a declarative sentence.
  • Question mark (?) ends a direct question.
  • Exclamation mark (!) expresses strong feeling or emphasis.
  • Comma (,) separates items, phrases or clauses where appropriate.
  • Colon (:) can introduce a list, explanation or elaboration.
  • Semicolon (;) can link closely related independent clauses.
  • Apostrophe (') can indicate possession or omitted letters.
  • Quotation marks can indicate direct speech or quoted material.

Common punctuation errors

Do not place a comma between a subject and its main verb without a grammatical reason.

Incorrect: The students in the classroom, are writing.

Correct: The students in the classroom are writing.

Use an apostrophe carefully. Students is plural, while student's indicates possession by one student and students' indicates possession by more than one student.

15. Spelling

JAMB may require candidates to distinguish between correctly and incorrectly spelt words. Candidates should be familiar with standard British English spelling.

Commonly confused spellings

  • Accommodation, not accomodation.
  • Necessary, not neccessary.
  • Separate, not seperate.
  • Privilege, not priviledge.
  • Receive, not recieve.
  • Maintenance, not maintainance.
  • Pronunciation, not pronounciation.

Be especially careful with words whose spelling does not match the way they are commonly pronounced.

16. Ordinary Usage

Ordinary usage refers to the normal or literal meaning of a word or expression in its usual context.

Example: The farmer planted maize in the field.

Here, planted has its ordinary meaning: putting a seed or plant into the ground.

17. Figurative Usage

Figurative usage occurs when words are used in a non-literal way to create a particular effect or meaning.

Example: The news shook the nation.

The nation was not physically shaken. The expression means that the news had a very strong impact on the people.

In JAMB questions, interpret figurative expressions according to the context rather than taking every word literally.

18. Idiomatic Usage

An idiom is a fixed expression whose overall meaning cannot always be obtained simply by adding the meanings of its individual words. The JAMB syllabus specifies that idioms tested should be formal expressions in Standard British English.

Common examples

  • At the eleventh hour — at the last possible moment.
  • To be in hot water — to be in trouble.
  • To call it a day — to stop working for the day.
  • To make ends meet — to manage financially.
  • To take something for granted — to fail to appreciate its value or assume it will always be available.
  • To turn a deaf ear — to refuse to listen.
  • To throw in the towel — to give up.
  • To break the ice — to make people feel more comfortable in a new or tense situation.

JAMB tip: Learn idioms as complete expressions and understand their meanings in sentences. Do not interpret them word for word.

19. Sentence Interpretation

Sentence interpretation questions test your ability to understand what a sentence means, especially when an expression has been highlighted or presented in an unusual form.

For example, if a sentence says that a candidate passed with flying colours, the expression means that the candidate passed very successfully.

To solve sentence interpretation questions:

  1. Read the entire sentence.
  2. Identify the key expression.
  3. Consider the context.
  4. Replace the expression mentally with each answer option.
  5. Choose the option that preserves the original meaning most accurately.

20. Sentence Completion

Sentence completion questions require you to select the word or expression that makes a sentence grammatically and logically correct.

Consider both grammar and meaning. An option may sound possible but still be grammatically incorrect.

Example: Neither the teacher nor the students ______ aware of the change.

  • A. was
  • B. were
  • C. is
  • D. has

The best answer is were because the verb agrees with the nearer subject, students, in this construction.

21. How to Approach Lexis and Structure Questions

  1. Read before answering: Never select an option before understanding the sentence.
  2. Identify the grammatical structure: Determine the subject, verb, object, complement and other important elements.
  3. Check the context: A word may have several meanings.
  4. Eliminate clearly wrong options: Remove answers that violate grammar, meaning, spelling or usage.
  5. Check agreement: Make sure subjects and verbs agree correctly.
  6. Check tense: Look for time expressions such as yesterday, already, since, tomorrow and by the time.
  7. Watch prepositions: Some verbs, adjectives and expressions require particular prepositions.
  8. Consider standard usage: Prefer the form accepted in Standard British English where the question requires it.

22. Worked Examples

Example 1: Synonym

The manager was reluctant to approve the proposal.

Which option is nearest in meaning to reluctant?

Answer: Unwilling.

Explanation: A reluctant person is unwilling or hesitant to do something.

Example 2: Antonym

The instructions were explicit.

Which option is opposite in meaning to explicit?

Answer: Vague.

Explanation: Explicit means clearly expressed, while vague means unclear or not precise.

Example 3: Concord

Each of the players ______ received a medal.

Answer: has.

Explanation: The subject is each, which is singular, even though players is plural.

Example 4: Question tag

You have completed the assignment, ______?

Answer: haven't you?

Explanation: The statement is positive and contains the auxiliary have, so the tag is negative: haven't you?

Example 5: Idiomatic usage

The principal decided to turn a deaf ear to the complaints.

Answer: Refused to listen to the complaints.

Explanation: The expression is idiomatic and does not mean that the principal literally became deaf.

23. Self-Assessment Checklist

Before considering this topic mastered, you should be able to:

  • identify synonyms and choose the appropriate synonym from context;
  • identify antonyms and distinguish contextual opposites;
  • recognise and distinguish common homonyms and homophones;
  • identify independent and dependent clauses;
  • recognise common sentence patterns;
  • identify major word classes and explain their functions;
  • distinguish tense from aspect;
  • apply subject-verb agreement correctly;
  • identify singular and plural forms;
  • form and use positive, comparative and superlative degrees correctly;
  • complete question tags accurately;
  • use common punctuation marks correctly;
  • recognise standard spellings;
  • distinguish ordinary, figurative and idiomatic meanings; and
  • interpret sentences accurately from their context.

24. Final JAMB Strategy

Lexis and Structure questions reward accuracy rather than guesswork. Build a strong vocabulary, revise common grammatical patterns, practise concord and sentence completion, and learn frequently tested idiomatic expressions. When faced with an unfamiliar word, use the surrounding words and the overall meaning of the sentence to infer its meaning. Always remember that the correct answer must fit both the grammar and the meaning of the sentence.

Key principle: In JAMB Use of English, context determines meaning. Always ask: What does this word or expression mean here?

lessons.html:
Oral Forms

Oral Forms is the part of JAMB Use of English that tests a candidate's knowledge of the sound system of English. It focuses on how words are pronounced rather than how they are written. The major areas covered are vowels, consonants and consonant clusters, rhymes and homophones, word stress, and intonation or emphatic stress.

For the UTME, a candidate should be able to distinguish different vowel and consonant sounds and identify the correct pronunciation or accentuation of words in isolation and in connected speech. The official JAMB syllabus specifically lists vowels (monophthongs and diphthongs), consonants including clusters, rhymes including homophones, word stress in monosyllabic and polysyllabic words, and intonation involving emphatic stress.

Learning Objectives

At the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • distinguish between different vowel sounds;
  • distinguish between different consonant sounds;
  • identify consonant clusters in words;
  • recognise words that rhyme;
  • distinguish homophones from words that merely look or sound similar;
  • identify the stressed syllable in monosyllabic and polysyllabic words;
  • recognise normal sentence stress and emphatic stress;
  • understand how intonation affects spoken English; and
  • answer JAMB Oral Forms questions by comparing sounds rather than spellings.

1. Understanding Speech Sounds

English spelling does not always represent pronunciation directly. The same letter can represent different sounds, while different letters can represent the same sound. For example, the letter a has different pronunciations in words such as cat, father and late. Therefore, in Oral Forms questions, do not rely only on the written form of a word. Listen mentally to the sound represented by the relevant letter or group of letters.

JAMB may present one word followed by several options and ask you to identify the option containing the same vowel or consonant sound as a particular sound in the given word.

2. Vowels

A vowel is a speech sound produced with a relatively open passage of air through the mouth. Unlike consonants, vowels are normally produced without complete closure or significant obstruction of the airflow.

The JAMB syllabus identifies two main vowel categories for Oral Forms: monophthongs and diphthongs.

2.1 Monophthongs

A monophthong is a vowel sound produced with a relatively stable tongue and mouth position throughout the sound. It is commonly called a pure vowel.

Examples include the vowel sounds heard in words such as sit, bed, cat, cup, food and father.

For examination purposes, the important point is that the vowel sound, not the spelling, determines the answer. Words containing the same letter may have different vowel sounds.

2.2 Diphthongs

A diphthong is a vowel sound in which the speech organs move from one vowel position towards another within the same syllable. It therefore involves a noticeable movement of the vowel quality.

Examples can be heard in words such as day, time, boy, house and go.

A common JAMB approach is to give a word and ask you to select another word containing the same vowel sound. The spelling may be different, so focus on pronunciation.

2.3 Vowel Length

Some English vowel contrasts involve differences in vowel length. A long vowel is generally held for a longer duration than a corresponding short vowel. This distinction can contribute to differences in meaning.

For example, compare the vowel quality and duration in pairs such as ship and sheep. The spelling difference is not the main issue in an Oral Forms question; the sound distinction is.

3. Consonants

A consonant is a speech sound produced with some degree of obstruction or narrowing of the airflow in the vocal tract. The obstruction may involve the lips, tongue, teeth or other speech organs.

Examples of consonant sounds occur at the beginning of pen, ten, go, ship, chair and van.

3.1 Voiced and Voiceless Consonants

One useful distinction is between voiced and voiceless consonants. A voiced consonant is produced with vibration of the vocal cords, while a voiceless consonant is produced without vocal-cord vibration.

Common pairs include /p/ and /b/, /t/ and /d/, /k/ and /g/, /f/ and /v/, and /s/ and /z/.

When answering a question on consonant sounds, compare the actual sound rather than the letter used to represent it.

3.2 Consonant Clusters

A consonant cluster is a sequence of two or more consonant sounds occurring together without an intervening vowel sound. Clusters can occur at the beginning, middle or end of words.

Examples include the initial clusters in school, black and three, and the final clusters in words such as asked, helped and texts.

Do not confuse a consonant cluster with a single consonant sound represented by two letters. For example, sh in ship represents one consonant sound, whereas the initial sounds in stop form a cluster.

4. Silent Letters

A silent letter is a letter that occurs in the spelling of a word but is not pronounced. English contains many words in which spelling and pronunciation differ.

Examples include the silent k in knife, the silent b in debt, and the silent w in write.

Silent letters are important because JAMB Oral Forms questions test pronunciation, not spelling. When comparing words, identify the sounds that are actually pronounced.

5. Rhymes

Rhyming words are words that have the same or closely matching final stressed vowel and following sound pattern. In examination questions, you may be asked to identify a word that rhymes with another word.

For example, light, night and right rhyme because they share the same ending sound pattern.

Words do not have to have the same spelling to rhyme. For example, blue and through have different spellings but share a rhyming sound.

5.1 Complete and Partial Rhymes

A complete rhyme has the same stressed vowel and the sounds following it. A partial rhyme has only a close similarity in some parts of the ending sound pattern.

In JAMB-style questions, concentrate on the sound of the final stressed syllable. Do not choose an answer simply because its spelling looks similar to the target word.

6. Homophones

Homophones are words that have the same pronunciation but different meanings and usually different spellings.

Common examples include right and write, sea and see, son and sun, and pair and pear.

Homophones should be distinguished from homographs. Homophones are identified primarily by sound, whereas homographs share the same spelling and may or may not have the same pronunciation.

7. Word Stress

Stress is the extra prominence given to a syllable when a word is pronounced. A stressed syllable is usually more prominent because of a combination of factors such as greater loudness, length, clearer vowel quality and pitch.

In Oral Forms, JAMB may require you to identify the syllable that receives the primary stress in a word or to choose a word with the same stress pattern as another word.

7.1 Monosyllabic Words

A monosyllabic word has only one syllable. Since there is only one syllable, it carries the word's main stress automatically.

Examples include book, school, friend, chair and write.

7.2 Polysyllabic Words

A polysyllabic word contains two or more syllables. One syllable normally receives greater prominence than the others.

For example, in TAble, the first syllable is prominent, while in beGIN, the second syllable is prominent. In longer words, the location of stress must be learned from the pronunciation of the individual word.

Some words change their stress pattern when their grammatical category changes. A familiar example is PREsent when used as a noun or adjective and preSENT when used as a verb. Such distinctions are useful in Oral Forms questions.

7.3 Stress and Word Formation

Stress can sometimes be affected by prefixes and suffixes, but there is no single rule that correctly predicts the stress of every English word. Therefore, avoid relying on oversimplified rules such as always stressing the first syllable or always stressing the syllable after a prefix.

The safest examination method is to learn the pronunciation and stress pattern of commonly tested words and compare the stressed syllable with the options provided.

8. Sentence Stress

Sentence stress is the normal placement of greater prominence on important content words in connected speech. Content words commonly include nouns, main verbs, adjectives and adverbs.

For example, in the sentence The STUDENT BOUGHT a NEW BOOK, the important information is normally carried by the content words. Function words such as articles, pronouns, auxiliary verbs and prepositions are often less prominent unless the speaker wants to emphasise them.

Sentence stress should not automatically be treated as emphatic stress. Normal sentence stress helps organise ordinary speech, while emphatic stress deliberately highlights a particular word.

9. Emphatic Stress

Emphatic stress involves placing unusual or stronger prominence on a word in an utterance in order to emphasise, correct or contrast information. This is specifically identified in the JAMB syllabus.

Consider the statement: John bought the blue shirt. If someone asks whether John bought the red shirt, the speaker may place emphatic stress on blue to correct the information. If someone asks whether Mary bought the shirt, the speaker may emphasise John.

The key principle is that changing the stressed word can change the particular piece of information being emphasised.

9.1 How to Answer Emphatic Stress Questions

When a JAMB question asks which word should receive emphatic stress, read the statement and determine the information that the speaker needs to correct or contrast.

Ask yourself: What part of the statement is being questioned, contradicted or corrected? That is usually the word that should receive the strongest emphasis.

10. Intonation

Intonation is the pattern of pitch movement in spoken language. The voice does not remain at one pitch throughout an utterance. Speakers raise or lower pitch to communicate grammatical meaning, attitude, emotion and emphasis.

10.1 Falling Intonation

Falling intonation is a movement of the voice from a higher pitch towards a lower pitch. It is commonly associated with complete statements, commands and many information questions.

For example, a speaker may use a falling pattern when saying a straightforward statement such as She is coming.

10.2 Rising Intonation

Rising intonation involves movement from a lower pitch towards a higher pitch. It is commonly associated with many yes-or-no questions and expressions of uncertainty or incompleteness.

For example, a speaker may use a rising pattern when asking a question such as Are you ready?

These are useful general patterns rather than absolute rules. Context, attitude and the speaker's intention can change the intonation used.

11. Pronunciation Versus Spelling

One of the most important lessons in Oral Forms is that spelling cannot always be trusted as a guide to pronunciation. English contains many words whose spelling is similar but whose sounds differ, as well as words whose spellings differ but whose sounds are similar or identical.

For example, food and good contain similar-looking spellings but different vowel sounds. Similarly, see and sea have different spellings but the same pronunciation.

Therefore, when solving Oral Forms questions, mentally pronounce the words and compare their sounds.

12. A Practical Method for JAMB Oral Forms Questions

Use the following procedure when answering an Oral Forms question:

  1. Read the target word carefully.
  2. Identify the particular sound or stress pattern being tested.
  3. Pronounce the target word mentally.
  4. Pronounce each option rather than judging by spelling.
  5. Compare only the relevant sound, syllable or stress pattern.
  6. Eliminate options that differ in the tested feature.
  7. Select the option with the same pronunciation feature.

13. Common Examination Traps

  • Choosing by spelling: Two words may look alike but contain different sounds.
  • Ignoring silent letters: A written letter may not contribute a sound.
  • Confusing letters with sounds: One letter can represent different sounds, and one sound can be represented by different spellings.
  • Ignoring syllables: Word-stress questions require attention to the stressed syllable.
  • Confusing sentence stress with emphatic stress: Normal sentence stress is not necessarily used to correct or contrast information.
  • Relying on spelling for rhymes: Rhyming is determined by sound, not by similar-looking endings.
  • Assuming one stress rule works for every word: English stress has patterns, but many individual words must be learned through correct pronunciation.

14. Worked Examples

Example 1: Vowel Sound

Question: Choose the word that contains the same vowel sound as the vowel sound in seat.

A. sit
B. beat
C. set
D. sat

Answer: B. beat.

Explanation: seat and beat contain the same long vowel sound. The other options contain different vowel sounds.

Example 2: Consonant Sound

Question: Choose the word that begins with the same consonant sound as fan.

A. van
B. phone
C. fine
D. pan

Answer: C. fine.

Explanation: fan and fine begin with the same consonant sound. van begins with a voiced consonant, while pan begins with a different consonant.

Example 3: Rhyme

Question: Which word rhymes with light?

A. late
B. let
C. right
D. lot

Answer: C. right.

Explanation: light and right have the same final stressed sound pattern.

Example 4: Homophones

Question: Which pair consists of homophones?

A. cut and cot
B. sea and see
C. food and foot
D. ship and sheep

Answer: B. sea and see.

Explanation: The two words are pronounced alike but have different meanings and spellings.

Example 5: Word Stress

Question: Which word has stress on the second syllable?

A. TAble
B. MARket
C. beGIN
D. DOCtor

Answer: C. beGIN.

Explanation: The second syllable receives the primary stress in begin.

Example 6: Emphatic Stress

Statement: Ada bought the red dress.

If the speaker wants to correct the information that the dress was blue, which word should receive emphatic stress?

Answer: red.

Explanation: The colour is the information being corrected or contrasted, so the colour word receives emphatic stress.

15. Self-Assessment

Test yourself without looking at the answers first.

  1. Which of the following contains a diphthong?
    A. cat
    B. bed
    C. boy
    D. cup
  2. Which pair contains homophones?
    A. son and sun
    B. sit and seat
    C. ship and sheep
    D. cut and cat
  3. Which word contains a consonant cluster at the beginning?
    A. school
    B. apple
    C. orange
    D. idea
  4. Which word has stress on the second syllable?
    A. TAble
    B. WINdow
    C. reLAX
    D. DOCtor
  5. If a speaker says, I ordered tea and wants to correct someone who thinks the speaker ordered coffee, which word should receive emphatic stress?

Answers to Self-Assessment

  1. C. boy contains a diphthong.
  2. A. son and sun are pronounced alike but have different meanings and spellings.
  3. A. school begins with a consonant cluster.
  4. C. reLAX has the primary stress on the second syllable.
  5. The word tea should receive emphatic stress because it is the information being contrasted with or corrected from coffee.

16. Final Revision Checklist

Before the examination, make sure you can explain the following:

  • the difference between monophthongs and diphthongs;
  • the difference between vowels and consonants;
  • what a consonant cluster is;
  • what silent letters are and why they matter in pronunciation;
  • what makes two words rhyme;
  • the meaning of homophones;
  • how word stress operates in monosyllabic and polysyllabic words;
  • the difference between normal sentence stress and emphatic stress;
  • the basic use of rising and falling intonation; and
  • why pronunciation, rather than spelling, should guide your answer in Oral Forms questions.

Conclusion

Oral Forms becomes easier when you stop treating English as a purely written language and begin to analyse it as a system of sounds. JAMB expects candidates to distinguish vowel and consonant types, recognise rhymes and homophones, identify stress patterns and understand emphasis in connected speech. Regularly pronounce words aloud, compare similar sounds, practise stress patterns and pay attention to silent letters. Most importantly, remember that the correct answer in an Oral Forms question is determined by the sound being tested, not simply by the way the word is spelt.
