lessons.html:
Oral Forms

Oral Forms is an important part of JAMB Use of English. It tests a candidate's ability to recognize and distinguish English speech sounds, pronunciation patterns, word stress, rhymes and intonation. According to the JAMB Use of English syllabus, the areas covered are vowels, consonants including consonant clusters, rhymes including homophones, word stress in monosyllabic and polysyllabic words, and intonation including emphatic stress.

The key point to remember is that English spelling does not always represent English pronunciation accurately. Two words may look different but have the same sound, while two words may contain the same letter but have different sounds. JAMB therefore tests the sound of a word rather than simply the letters used to spell it.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • distinguish between vowels and consonants;
  • identify monophthongs and diphthongs;
  • recognize important English consonant sounds and consonant clusters;
  • identify words that rhyme;
  • distinguish homophones from ordinary spelling similarities;
  • identify stressed syllables in monosyllabic and polysyllabic words;
  • understand how stress can change the meaning or grammatical function of some words;
  • identify emphatic stress in connected speech; and
  • recognize common patterns of English intonation.

1. Understanding Speech Sounds

A speech sound is a sound produced by the human speech organs and used in a language to communicate meaning. English has many speech sounds, and these sounds can be broadly divided into vowels and consonants.

The distinction is based mainly on how the air from the lungs moves through the mouth and vocal tract. In vowel production, the airflow is relatively unobstructed. In consonant production, the airflow is obstructed or restricted at some point.

Vowels and Consonants

A vowel is produced with relatively free passage of air through the mouth. Examples include the vowel sounds in words such as sit, seat, cup and food.

A consonant is produced when the airflow is completely blocked or significantly restricted at some point in the vocal tract. Examples include the sounds represented by p, b, t, d, k, g, f and v.

2. Vowels

The JAMB syllabus identifies two major vowel categories for Oral Forms: monophthongs and diphthongs.

2.1 Monophthongs

A monophthong is a vowel sound produced with a relatively steady tongue and mouth position throughout its pronunciation. It is sometimes called a pure vowel because the sound does not involve a significant movement from one vowel position to another.

Examples of English monophthongs include the vowel sounds heard in words such as ship, bed, cat, cup, hot, food and bird.

In JAMB questions, attention should be paid to the sound represented by a word rather than the spelling of its vowel letters. The same letter can represent different vowel sounds in different words.

Examples of Vowel Sound Differences

  • ship and sheep contain different vowel sounds.
  • full and fool contain different vowel sounds.
  • bed and bad contain different vowel sounds.
  • cut and cart contain different vowel sounds.

When solving a question, do not assume that words with similar spellings contain the same vowel sound.

2.2 Diphthongs

A diphthong is a vowel sound that involves a noticeable movement from one vowel position toward another within the same syllable. The quality of the sound changes as it is produced.

Common examples occur in words such as face, goat, time, boy, house and near.

For examination purposes, learn to recognize the sound rather than memorizing only the spelling pattern. A particular letter combination may represent different sounds in different words.

Monophthong Versus Diphthong

FeatureMonophthongDiphthong
Movement of vowel qualityRelatively steadyMoves from one vowel quality toward another
Number of vowel qualities involvedOne relatively stable qualityTwo vowel qualities within one syllable
ExampleThe vowel in sitThe vowel in time

3. Consonants

Consonants are speech sounds produced with some degree of obstruction or restriction of the airflow. They can be distinguished by the place and manner of articulation and, in many cases, by whether the vocal cords vibrate.

3.1 Voiced and Voiceless Consonants

A voiced consonant is produced with vibration of the vocal cords, while a voiceless consonant is produced without vocal-cord vibration.

Some consonants occur in voiced and voiceless pairs. For example, the sounds represented by p and b, t and d, k and g, and f and v differ partly in voicing.

A useful self-test is to place your fingers gently on your throat while producing the sounds. A vibration indicates voicing.

3.2 Consonant Sounds and Spelling

The number of letters in a word does not necessarily equal the number of consonant sounds. A single letter may represent a sound, while two or more letters may work together to represent one sound.

For example, the spelling sh represents one consonant sound in ship. Similarly, ch represents a consonant sound in chair.

This is why Oral English questions should be approached through pronunciation rather than spelling alone.

3.3 Consonant Clusters

A consonant cluster is a sequence of two or more consonant sounds occurring together without a vowel sound between them. Clusters can occur at the beginning, middle or end of words.

Examples include the initial clusters in play, street and bread, and final clusters in words such as asked and helped.

Be careful not to insert an extra vowel sound into a consonant cluster. In examination questions, you may be required to identify the word with a particular cluster or determine whether two words contain the same consonant pattern.

4. Rhymes

Rhyming words are words that have the same or closely matching sounds from the final stressed vowel onward. In examination questions, the spelling of the words may be different even when their sounds rhyme.

For example, light, night and right rhyme because their final stressed sound patterns are alike.

However, words that have similar spelling do not necessarily rhyme. The correct approach is to pronounce the words and compare their sounds.

How to Identify Rhyming Words

  1. Pronounce the words aloud.
  2. Locate the final stressed vowel sound.
  3. Compare the sounds that follow it.
  4. Ignore differences in spelling when the pronunciation is the same.

Examples

  • day rhymes with say.
  • rain rhymes with train.
  • food rhymes with mood.
  • rough does not rhyme with though, despite the similar spelling ending.

5. Homophones

Homophones are words that have the same pronunciation but different meanings, and often different spellings.

Common examples include:

Word 1Word 2Meaning Difference
rightwriteright can mean correct or a direction; write means to produce words in written form.
seaseesea refers to a large body of salt water; see means to perceive with the eyes.
flowerflourflower is the reproductive structure of a plant; flour is a powder used in cooking.
pairpearpair means two things considered together; pear is a type of fruit.

In JAMB, homophone questions test whether you can recognize that identical pronunciation does not necessarily mean identical spelling or meaning.

6. Word Stress

Word stress is the extra prominence given to one syllable in a word. A stressed syllable is usually more prominent because of a combination of greater loudness, longer duration, clearer vowel quality and pitch.

JAMB specifically includes stress in monosyllabic and polysyllabic words. You therefore need to know how stress operates both in short words and in longer words.

6.1 Monosyllabic Words

A monosyllabic word contains only one syllable. Since there is only one syllable, there is no choice between stressed and unstressed syllables within the word.

Examples include book, school, chair, friend and work.

6.2 Polysyllabic Words

A polysyllabic word contains two or more syllables. One syllable normally receives primary stress.

Examples include TAble, beGIN, PREsent, reLAX and eduCATION. The capital letters here simply indicate the syllable receiving stronger stress.

Do not assume that stress always falls on the first syllable. English stress patterns vary from word to word and sometimes change when a word changes grammatical category.

6.3 Stress and Word Class

Some English words change their primary stress when they are used as different parts of speech. A common pattern is found with some noun-verb pairs.

  • PREsent as a noun can mean a gift.
  • preSENT as a verb means to give, show or introduce something.
  • REcord as a noun refers to stored information or an account of something.
  • reCORD as a verb means to make a record.

Such patterns are useful because JAMB may ask you to identify the word whose stress pattern differs from the others.

7. Emphatic Stress

Emphatic stress is the placement of normal stress on a particular word in an utterance to emphasize, correct or contrast information. This is specifically mentioned in the JAMB syllabus.

Consider the sentence: John bought the book. Depending on which word is emphasized, the speaker can communicate different meanings.

  • JOHN bought the book. This contrasts John with another possible person.
  • John BOUGHT the book. This contrasts buying with another action such as borrowing.
  • John bought THE book. This can contrast that particular book with another one.
  • John bought the BOOK. This can contrast the book with another object.

The grammatical words in the sentence remain the same, but changing the stressed word changes the information the speaker wants the listener to notice.

8. Intonation

Intonation refers to the pattern of pitch movement in spoken language. Pitch is the perceived highness or lowness of the voice. Intonation helps speakers communicate whether they are making a statement, asking a question, expressing surprise, showing uncertainty or conveying another attitude.

8.1 Falling Intonation

Falling intonation occurs when the pitch moves downward toward the end of an utterance. It is commonly associated with ordinary statements, commands and many information questions.

Examples include:

  • The meeting is over.
  • Where are you going?
  • Close the door.

The exact intonation used in natural speech can depend on context, so the purpose of the utterance must always be considered.

8.2 Rising Intonation

Rising intonation occurs when the pitch rises toward the end of an utterance. It is commonly associated with many yes-or-no questions and can also indicate uncertainty, incompleteness or a request for confirmation.

For example, a speaker may use rising intonation when asking: Are you coming?

8.3 Intonation and Meaning

Changing the intonation of the same sequence of words can affect how the listener interprets the speaker's intention. A statement may sound like a question when spoken with an appropriate rising pitch, while a falling pattern can make an utterance sound more final.

In JAMB questions, concentrate on the relationship between the intonation pattern and the communicative purpose of the utterance.

9. Sound Versus Spelling

One of the most important principles in Oral Forms is that spelling and pronunciation are not the same thing.

For example, the letter combination ough has different pronunciations in words such as though, through, rough and cough. Therefore, identifying a sound from spelling alone can lead to an incorrect answer.

Similarly, words such as know and no have the same pronunciation but different meanings and spellings. This makes them useful examples when studying homophones.

10. A Practical Method for Answering JAMB Oral Forms Questions

When you encounter an Oral Forms question, use the following procedure:

  1. Read all the options carefully. Do not select an answer based only on spelling.
  2. Pronounce each word mentally or quietly. Focus on the actual sounds.
  3. Identify the target feature. Determine whether the question concerns a vowel, consonant, rhyme, homophone, stress or intonation.
  4. Compare the relevant sound. Ignore unrelated parts of the word.
  5. Check the syllable or stress pattern. This is especially important in polysyllabic words.
  6. Eliminate options that do not match. If three options have the same sound pattern and one differs, the different one is often the answer.
  7. Confirm by pronunciation. Before choosing, say the words again and listen for the precise difference.

11. Common JAMB Oral Forms Question Patterns

Pattern A: Same Vowel Sound

You may be given a word and asked to select another word containing the same vowel sound.

Strategy: pronounce the target word and compare only the vowel sound in the relevant syllable.

Pattern B: Different Consonant Sound

You may be asked to identify the word whose underlined consonant represents a different sound from the others.

Strategy: isolate the consonant sound represented by the relevant letters rather than comparing the spelling.

Pattern C: Rhyming Words

You may be given a word and several options and asked to identify the word that rhymes with it.

Strategy: compare the sounds from the final stressed vowel onward.

Pattern D: Homophones

You may be required to identify a word that has the same pronunciation as another word but a different spelling or meaning.

Strategy: pronounce the words. Do not judge them by their written appearance.

Pattern E: Word Stress

You may be asked to select the option with a different stress pattern or identify the syllable that receives primary stress.

Strategy: divide the word into syllables and pronounce it naturally. Listen for the syllable that receives the greatest prominence.

Pattern F: Emphatic Stress

You may be given a sentence in which one word is written in capital letters and asked what the emphasis means.

Strategy: ask what information the emphasized word corrects, contrasts or highlights.

Pattern G: Intonation

You may be asked to identify the appropriate intonation for an utterance.

Strategy: first determine whether the utterance is a statement, command, yes-or-no question, information question or another type of expression. Then consider the likely pitch movement.

12. Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Do not rely on spelling. English spelling is not a reliable guide to pronunciation in every case.
  • Do not confuse letters with sounds. Two letters can represent one sound, and one letter can represent different sounds in different words.
  • Do not confuse rhyming with identical spelling. Words rhyme because of their sounds, not because they look alike.
  • Do not confuse homophones with synonyms. Homophones have the same pronunciation but different meanings; synonyms have similar meanings.
  • Do not ignore syllables when studying stress. First divide longer words into their syllables.
  • Do not assume that every question has a simple rising-or-falling rule. Context affects intonation in natural speech.
  • Do not pronounce words according to spelling alone. Train yourself to recognize common English pronunciation patterns.

13. Self-Tutoring Practice

Before looking for the answer to any Oral Forms question, pronounce every option and explain the difference to yourself. This develops the listening and discrimination skills that the topic requires.

Practice 1: Vowels

Which word contains the same vowel sound as the vowel in seat?

  • A. sit
  • B. beat
  • C. set
  • D. sat

Answer: B. beat. The vowel sound in seat is the same as the vowel sound in beat.

Practice 2: Rhymes

Which word rhymes with light?

  • A. late
  • B. let
  • C. right
  • D. lot

Answer: C. right. Light and right have the same final stressed sound pattern.

Practice 3: Homophones

Which pair consists of homophones?

  • A. food and foot
  • B. sea and see
  • C. cut and cot
  • D. ship and sheep

Answer: B. sea and see. They have the same pronunciation but different spellings and meanings.

Practice 4: Consonants

Which pair contains consonant sounds that form a voiced and voiceless pair?

  • A. p and b
  • B. m and n
  • C. l and r
  • D. w and y

Answer: A. p and b. The two sounds differ in voicing.

Practice 5: Stress

Which word has a different stress pattern from the others?

  • A. PREsent
  • B. TAble
  • C. reLAX
  • D. DOCtor

Answer: C. reLAX. The primary stress falls on the second syllable, while the other examples have primary stress on the first syllable.

Practice 6: Emphatic Stress

Consider the sentence: Mary borrowed my book. If the speaker emphasizes MARY, what is most likely being emphasized?

  • A. The object borrowed
  • B. The person who borrowed it
  • C. The action of borrowing
  • D. The ownership of the book

Answer: B. The person who borrowed it. Emphasis on Mary can contrast her with another possible person.

14. Quick Revision Summary

  • Vowels are produced with relatively unobstructed airflow.
  • Monophthongs are relatively steady vowel sounds.
  • Diphthongs involve movement from one vowel quality toward another within a syllable.
  • Consonants involve some obstruction or restriction of airflow.
  • Consonant clusters contain two or more consonant sounds occurring together without an intervening vowel sound.
  • Rhymes are based on matching sound patterns, not necessarily matching spelling.
  • Homophones have the same pronunciation but different meanings and often different spellings.
  • Word stress gives greater prominence to one syllable in a word.
  • Emphatic stress highlights a particular word to emphasize, correct or contrast information.
  • Intonation is the pattern of pitch movement across an utterance.
  • Falling intonation is commonly associated with statements, commands and many information questions.
  • Rising intonation is commonly associated with many yes-or-no questions and can signal uncertainty or a request for confirmation.
  • Always distinguish sound from spelling when answering Oral Forms questions.

15. Final Examination Tip

The most effective way to prepare for Oral Forms is to practise with your ears as well as your eyes. Read words aloud, compare their sounds, divide longer words into syllables and deliberately listen for vowel quality, consonant differences, rhyme and stress. When a question appears difficult, do not be distracted by similar spellings. JAMB's syllabus focuses on the candidate's ability to distinguish speech sounds and identify correct accentuation, so pronunciation should guide your answer.

Mastering these distinctions will make questions on vowels, consonants, rhymes, homophones, stress and intonation much easier to approach.

lessons.title: Ordinary, Figurative and Idiomatic Usage
lessons.html:
Ordinary, Figurative and Idiomatic Usage

Ordinary, figurative and idiomatic usage are important aspects of English vocabulary and expression. In JAMB Use of English, candidates are expected to understand words and expressions according to the context in which they occur. An expression may have a direct meaning, an imaginative meaning, or a special meaning that is established by common usage.

The JAMB Use of English syllabus places ordinary usage, figurative usage and idiomatic usage under Lexis and Structure. Candidates are expected to identify words and expressions in their ordinary, figurative and idiomatic contexts and interpret the information conveyed in sentences. JAMB also specifies that the idioms tested should be formal and expressed in standard British English.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • Explain the difference between ordinary, figurative and idiomatic usage.
  • Identify whether an expression is being used literally or figuratively.
  • Interpret figurative expressions correctly from their contexts.
  • Recognise common formal English idioms.
  • Determine the meaning of an idiom from the context in which it occurs.
  • Distinguish an idiom from an ordinary combination of words.
  • Choose the option that gives the correct meaning of an expression in a JAMB-style question.

1. Ordinary Usage

Ordinary usage is the normal, direct or literal use of a word or expression. The words mean what they ordinarily say, without an additional imaginative or special interpretation.

For example, in the sentence "The boy opened the door.", the word door refers to a physical door. The statement has a direct meaning.

Other examples include:

  • "The farmer planted maize in the field." The word planted has its ordinary meaning of putting seeds into the soil.
  • "Ada carried the bag to school." The sentence describes the physical action of carrying a bag.
  • "The glass fell from the table." The glass is an actual physical object that fell.

In ordinary usage, the meaning of the sentence can usually be understood directly from the words used.

2. Figurative Usage

Figurative usage occurs when words are used beyond their literal or ordinary meanings to create an image, comparison, emphasis or special effect. The expression should not normally be interpreted exactly as the individual words suggest.

Figurative language is common in everyday English as well as in literature, speeches, newspapers and examinations.

Example 1: "The news broke his heart."

The expression does not mean that the person's physical heart was broken. It means that the news caused him great emotional pain or sadness.

Example 2: "The classroom was a zoo."

The classroom is not literally a zoo. The statement means that the classroom was extremely noisy, disorderly or difficult to control.

Example 3: "She has a heart of stone."

This does not mean that her heart is physically made of stone. It means that she is considered unfeeling, cruel or lacking in sympathy.

Example 4: "The news spread like wildfire."

This means that the news spread very quickly. It does not mean that actual fire spread through the news.

3. Literal and Figurative Meaning

A useful way of answering JAMB questions is to ask whether the words should be understood literally or according to an extended meaning suggested by the context.

ExpressionLiteral MeaningFigurative Meaning
He has a cold hand.His hand has a low temperature.Depending on context, it may describe an unwelcoming or unfriendly manner.
The man has a sharp tongue.A tongue that is physically sharp.The man speaks harshly or critically.
She is carrying a heavy burden.She is physically carrying something heavy.She is dealing with a serious responsibility or problem.
The politician washed his hands of the matter.He physically washed his hands.He refused to accept responsibility or involvement.

Important: Context determines whether an expression is ordinary or figurative. Do not assume that an expression is figurative simply because it can have a figurative meaning.

4. Common Types of Figurative Expression

JAMB questions may require you to understand the meaning of an expression rather than identify its literary name. Therefore, the most important skill is understanding the meaning conveyed by the expression in context.

Simile

A simile compares two things using words such as like or as.

  • "The baby slept like a log." This means the baby slept very deeply.
  • "He is as brave as a lion." This means he is very brave.

Metaphor

A metaphor describes one thing as if it were another in order to suggest a shared quality.

  • "The young man is a shining star." This suggests that he is very successful, talented or outstanding.
  • "Time is a thief." This suggests that time gradually takes away opportunities, youth or moments without being noticed.

Personification

Personification gives human qualities or actions to non-human things.

  • "The wind whispered through the trees." Wind cannot literally whisper like a human being, but the expression describes its soft sound.
  • "The sun smiled on the village." The sun cannot literally smile; the expression suggests pleasant sunshine.

Hyperbole

Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration used for emphasis. It is not intended to be understood literally.

  • "I have told you a thousand times." This usually means the speaker has repeated the information many times.
  • "He has a mountain of work to do." This means he has a very large amount of work.

5. Idiomatic Usage

An idiom is a fixed expression whose established meaning is different from the literal meaning suggested by its individual words. Idioms must generally be understood as complete expressions.

For example, "to spill the beans" does not normally mean to scatter beans. It means to reveal a secret or disclose information that was supposed to remain secret.

Another example is "to make ends meet". It does not refer literally to joining two ends together. It means to have just enough money to pay for one's necessary expenses.

6. Ordinary Expression versus Idiom

The same words may sometimes be used literally or idiomatically. Context is therefore essential.

SentenceUsageMeaning
She broke the glass.OrdinaryShe damaged the glass physically.
She broke the news to me.IdiomaticShe told me the news, usually unpleasant or important news.
He kicked the bucket.IdiomaticHe died.
He kicked the bucket under the table.OrdinaryHe physically kicked a bucket.

This distinction is particularly important in objective questions. The presence of familiar words does not necessarily mean that the sentence should be interpreted literally.

7. Common Formal English Idioms

The following expressions are useful for JAMB preparation. Learn both the expression and its established meaning, and pay attention to how each is used in a sentence.

IdiomMeaningExample
At daggers drawnTo be extremely hostile towards one anotherThe two neighbours are at daggers drawn over the boundary dispute.
At the eleventh hourAt the last possible momentHe submitted the application at the eleventh hour.
Bear in mindRemember or considerBear in mind that the examination begins at eight o'clock.
Beat about the bushAvoid coming directly to the pointStop beating about the bush and tell us what happened.
Break the iceMake people feel more relaxed in a new or uncomfortable situationThe chairman told a joke to break the ice.
Bring to lightReveal or discover something previously hiddenThe investigation brought several facts to light.
By and largeGenerally; on the wholeBy and large, the candidates performed well.
Call it a dayStop working for the dayWe have completed the major tasks, so let us call it a day.
Call to accountDemand an explanation or hold someone responsibleThe manager called the accountant to account for the missing funds.
Come to lightBecome known or discoveredNew evidence came to light during the investigation.
Cut cornersDo something cheaply or carelessly by avoiding necessary stepsThe contractor was accused of cutting corners.
Fall throughFail to happen or be completedThe proposed agreement fell through at the last minute.
Get out of handBecome difficult to controlThe argument quickly got out of hand.
Give someone the benefit of the doubtAccept that someone may be innocent when there is uncertaintyI will give him the benefit of the doubt until we know the facts.
Go the extra mileMake an additional effortThe teacher went the extra mile to help the students.
In black and whiteIn written or clearly documented formThe agreement is in black and white.
In the long runEventually; over a long periodHard work will benefit you in the long run.
Keep an eye onWatch or monitor carefullyPlease keep an eye on the children.
Leave no stone unturnedMake every possible effort to find or achieve somethingThe police left no stone unturned in their search for the suspect.
Make ends meetHave enough money to meet one's basic expensesMany families struggle to make ends meet.
On the spur of the momentWithout prior planningShe accepted the invitation on the spur of the moment.
Put one's foot downRefuse firmly to allow somethingThe principal put his foot down and rejected the proposal.
Read between the linesLook for a hidden or implied meaningIf you read between the lines, you will understand his real intention.
See eye to eyeAgree completelyThe two leaders do not always see eye to eye.
Take to taskCriticise or rebuke someone for a faultThe supervisor took the worker to task for his negligence.
The last strawThe final problem that makes a situation intolerableHis repeated lateness was the last straw.
Through thick and thinThrough good and bad circumstancesShe supported her friend through thick and thin.
Turn a deaf earRefuse to listen or pay attentionThe authorities turned a deaf ear to the complaints.
Under the weatherFeeling unwellI am feeling under the weather today.
Weather the stormSurvive a difficult periodThe company managed to weather the storm.

8. Idioms in Context

In a JAMB question, you may be given an idiom in a sentence and asked to select the option that best explains it. The correct answer is the one that preserves the intended meaning of the complete expression.

Example: The chairman decided to put his foot down on the matter.

The expression put his foot down means to take a firm stand or refuse to change one's decision.

Therefore, if the options are:

  1. place his foot on the ground
  2. walk away from the matter
  3. take a firm stand
  4. avoid discussing the matter

The correct answer is 3. take a firm stand.

9. How to Identify Figurative or Idiomatic Meaning

Use the following steps when answering examination questions:

  1. Read the whole sentence. Do not interpret the expression in isolation.
  2. Check the literal meaning. Ask yourself whether the literal interpretation makes sense in the context.
  3. Look for an established expression. If the combination of words has a recognised special meaning, it may be an idiom.
  4. Consider the surrounding words. The context often provides clues to the intended meaning.
  5. Replace the expression mentally. Substitute a simple phrase for the expression and see which option gives the same meaning.
  6. Reject distractors based only on individual words. JAMB may provide an option that represents the literal meaning of an idiom rather than its actual meaning.

10. Important Difference Between Figurative Language and Idioms

Figurative language and idioms are related, but they are not exactly the same.

Figurative usage generally involves using language in a non-literal way to communicate an idea, image or comparison. It may be newly created by a speaker or writer and understood from the context.

Idiomatic usage involves an established expression whose meaning is conventionally recognised by users of the language. The expression often cannot be understood accurately by interpreting every word literally.

For example, "The news broke his heart" is a figurative expression because broke his heart conveys emotional pain rather than physical damage. "Make ends meet" is an idiom because the expression has an established meaning: to have enough money to cover one's necessary expenses.

11. Context Is More Important Than Memorisation Alone

Memorising idioms is useful, but JAMB questions test your ability to interpret expressions in context. A word or group of words can have different meanings in different sentences.

Compare these examples:

  • "The man broke the window." This is ordinary usage.
  • "The man broke the news to his family." Here, broke the news means announced or revealed the news.
  • "The glass was on the table." This is ordinary usage.
  • "The politician was caught with his hand in the cookie jar." The expression suggests that the politician was caught doing something wrong or dishonest, rather than literally having a hand in a jar.

12. Common Examination Traps

Candidates should be careful of the following traps:

  • Literal distractors: An option may give the physical meaning of the words instead of the idiomatic meaning.
  • Partially correct meanings: An option may be related to the expression but not accurately represent its meaning.
  • Wrong context: An idiom may have several related expressions, so choose the meaning that fits the sentence.
  • Unnecessary interpretation: Do not create a complicated meaning when a simple established meaning fits the sentence.
  • Incorrect expression: Be familiar with the exact form of common idioms. Changing a word may change or destroy the idiomatic expression.

13. JAMB-Style Practice Questions

Question 1: The principal decided to put his foot down when the students continued to disobey the rule. This means that the principal decided to

  1. stamp his foot angrily
  2. take a firm stand
  3. leave the school
  4. punish every student

Answer: 2. Take a firm stand.

Question 2: The investigation finally brought the truth to light. This means that the investigation

  1. made the truth visible in the daytime
  2. hid the truth
  3. revealed the truth
  4. changed the truth

Answer: 3. Revealed the truth.

Question 3: The two brothers have been at daggers drawn since the disagreement. This means that they have been

  1. very friendly
  2. extremely hostile
  3. physically fighting with knives
  4. working together

Answer: 2. Extremely hostile.

Question 4: The committee left no stone unturned in its search for the missing document. This means that the committee

  1. searched only under stones
  2. made every possible effort
  3. gave up the search
  4. searched outside the country

Answer: 2. Made every possible effort.

Question 5: In the sentence, "The news spread like wildfire," the expression like wildfire means

  1. slowly and carefully
  2. quickly and widely
  3. secretly and quietly
  4. only among villagers

Answer: 2. Quickly and widely.

Question 6: The family is struggling to make ends meet. This means that the family is struggling to

  1. join two pieces together
  2. save a large amount of money
  3. meet its necessary expenses
  4. start a new business

Answer: 3. Meet its necessary expenses.

14. Quick Revision Guide

  • Ordinary usage: Words have their direct or literal meanings.
  • Figurative usage: Words communicate an extended, imaginative or non-literal meaning.
  • Idiom: A fixed expression with an established meaning that may differ from the literal meanings of its individual words.
  • Context: Always use the surrounding sentence to determine the intended meaning.
  • JAMB focus: Be able to identify and interpret expressions in ordinary, figurative and idiomatic contexts.
  • Idioms: Give special attention to formal idioms expressed in standard British English.

15. Self-Assessment

Before leaving this lesson, you should be able to explain the difference between ordinary, figurative and idiomatic usage without assistance. You should also be able to interpret common expressions when they appear in unfamiliar sentences.

As a final test, explain the meaning of each expression below:

  1. At the eleventh hour
  2. Beat about the bush
  3. By and large
  4. Cut corners
  5. Get out of hand
  6. Go the extra mile
  7. Read between the lines
  8. See eye to eye
  9. Take to task
  10. Turn a deaf ear

Suggested answers: 1. At the last possible moment; 2. Avoid coming directly to the point; 3. Generally or on the whole; 4. Avoid necessary steps in order to save time, money or effort; 5. Become difficult to control; 6. Make an additional effort; 7. Look for an implied meaning; 8. Agree completely; 9. Criticise or rebuke; 10. Refuse to listen or pay attention.

Key Takeaway

The safest approach to ordinary, figurative and idiomatic usage questions is to focus on meaning in context. Do not automatically choose the literal meaning of an expression. First determine whether the words are being used normally, figuratively or as an established idiom, then select the option that gives the meaning intended by the sentence.

lessons.subject: english
lessons.title: Punctuation and Standard Spelling
lessons.html:
Punctuation and Standard Spelling

Punctuation and spelling are important parts of effective written English. In the JAMB Use of English syllabus, punctuation and spelling are included under Lexis and Structure. Candidates are expected to be able to differentiate between correct and incorrect punctuation and spelling.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • identify the major punctuation marks and explain their functions;
  • use punctuation marks correctly in sentences;
  • distinguish between correctly and incorrectly punctuated sentences;
  • recognise standard British-English spelling forms commonly used in Nigerian academic English;
  • identify commonly misspelled words and correct spelling errors;
  • answer JAMB-style questions involving punctuation and spelling.

1. What Is Punctuation?

Punctuation refers to the system of marks used in writing to separate ideas, indicate pauses, show relationships between words and clauses, and make the intended meaning of a sentence clear.

Compare these examples:

Without punctuation: Let us eat students.

With punctuation: Let us eat, students.

The comma changes the meaning completely. This shows why correct punctuation is essential in written communication.

2. The Full Stop (.)

A full stop is used mainly at the end of a complete declarative or imperative sentence.

Examples:

  • The candidates entered the examination hall.
  • Read the passage carefully.
  • JAMB conducts the UTME every year.

A full stop may also occur in some abbreviations, although modern usage often omits full stops from certain abbreviations.

3. The Comma (,)

The comma is one of the most frequently tested punctuation marks. It separates elements within a sentence and helps to prevent ambiguity.

Uses of the Comma

a. To separate items in a list

She bought books, pens, pencils and notebooks.

b. To separate a vocative expression

Chinedu, come here.

Students, listen carefully.

c. After an introductory word or phrase

However, the candidate continued with the examination.

After the lecture, the students returned to their classrooms.

d. To separate coordinate clauses in appropriate constructions

The rain stopped, and the candidates resumed the examination.

e. To set off non-essential information

Mr Okafor, the principal of the school, addressed the students.

The information between the commas is additional information about Mr Okafor.

Important JAMB Tip

Do not insert a comma simply because you hear a pause when reading a sentence. The grammatical relationship between the words and clauses should determine whether a comma is required.

4. The Semicolon (;)

A semicolon is stronger than a comma but weaker than a full stop. It can connect closely related independent clauses without using a conjunction.

Example: The examination was difficult; many candidates nevertheless performed well.

It can also separate items in a complicated list, especially when the items already contain commas.

5. The Colon (:)

A colon is commonly used to introduce an explanation, list, quotation or conclusion that follows from what comes before it.

Examples:

  • Bring the following items: a pencil, an eraser and your examination slip.
  • She had one objective: to pass the examination.
  • The teacher made an important announcement: the test would begin at noon.

6. The Apostrophe (')

The apostrophe is mainly used to show possession and omission of letters in contractions.

Apostrophe for Possession

  • The student's book is on the table.
  • The teachers' office is nearby.
  • James's pen is missing.

For a singular noun, an apostrophe is generally placed before the s. For a regular plural noun ending in s, the apostrophe normally comes after the s.

Apostrophe in Contractions

  • do not → don't
  • cannot → can't
  • it is → it's
  • they are → they're

Important: Do not confuse its with it's. Its indicates possession, while it's means it is or, in some contexts, it has.

Example: The dog wagged its tail. / It's raining.

7. The Question Mark (?)

A question mark is placed at the end of a direct question.

Examples:

  • What time does the examination begin?
  • Did you submit your application?
  • Why was the candidate absent?

Do not use a question mark after an indirect question.

Correct: He asked me where I lived.

Incorrect: He asked me where I lived?

8. The Exclamation Mark (!)

The exclamation mark is used after an expression showing strong emotion, surprise, excitement, pain or emphasis.

Examples:

  • What a wonderful performance!
  • Be careful!
  • That is unbelievable!

In formal academic writing, excessive use of the exclamation mark should be avoided.

9. Quotation Marks

Quotation marks are used to indicate direct speech or words reproduced exactly from another source.

Example: The teacher said, "Read the instructions carefully."

In dialogue, quotation marks help distinguish a speaker's exact words from the rest of the sentence.

10. The Hyphen (-)

A hyphen joins words or parts of words. It is commonly used in some compound words and compound modifiers.

Examples:

  • well-known writer
  • part-time student
  • mother-in-law
  • twenty-one

Do not confuse the hyphen with the longer dash used for other purposes.

11. Parentheses ( )

Parentheses are used to enclose additional information that is not essential to the main structure of a sentence.

Example: The candidate arrived early (about thirty minutes before the examination began).

12. Capitalisation

Correct punctuation also works together with correct capitalisation. The first word of a sentence should begin with a capital letter. Proper nouns, names of people and places, days, months and official names generally require capital letters.

Examples:

  • Monday
  • Nigeria
  • Lagos
  • English Language
  • JAMB

13. What Is Standard Spelling?

Standard spelling refers to the accepted conventional way of writing words in a particular variety of English. Nigerian academic English generally follows British English conventions, so candidates should be familiar with standard British spellings.

14. Common British-English Spellings

Some words commonly written differently in American English have British forms that candidates should recognise.

  • colour, not color
  • centre, not center
  • favour, not favor
  • honour, not honor
  • labour, not labor
  • organisation, not organization
  • programme, not program when referring to an organised event or course
  • travelling, not traveling
  • cancelled, not canceled
  • defence, not defense
  • licence as a noun, while license is commonly used as the verb in British English

15. Commonly Misspelled Words

JAMB-style spelling questions may test words whose spelling is easily confused. Learn the correct forms rather than relying only on pronunciation.

  • separate — not seperate
  • definite — not definately
  • necessary — not neccessary
  • accommodation — not accomodation
  • privilege — not priviledge
  • government — not goverment
  • environment — not enviroment
  • embarrass — not embarass
  • occurrence — not occurence
  • recommend — not recomend
  • beginning — not begining
  • successful — not succesful

16. Common Spelling Patterns to Remember

-ie and -ei

Many learners confuse ie and ei. Memorise common words individually.

  • believe
  • receive
  • ceiling
  • piece

Double Consonants

Pay attention to words containing double consonants.

  • accommodation
  • committee
  • embarrass
  • necessary
  • successful

Words Ending in -ful

The suffix -ful usually contains one l at the end.

  • beautiful
  • careful
  • successful
  • useful

Do not automatically write -full at the end of such words.

17. Words Commonly Confused Because of Spelling

Some words look or sound similar but have different meanings.

  • advice — a noun meaning guidance; advise — a verb meaning to give guidance.
  • practice — commonly used as a noun; practise is the British-English verb.
  • principal — a person in charge or something important; principle — a fundamental rule or belief.
  • stationery — writing materials; stationary — not moving.
  • complement — something that completes or goes well with something; compliment — praise.
  • affect — commonly a verb meaning to influence; effect — commonly a noun meaning result.
  • their — possessive form; there — refers to a place or introduces an expression; they're — they are.
  • your — possessive form; you're — you are.

18. How JAMB May Test Punctuation and Spelling

Questions may require you to identify the correctly punctuated or correctly spelt option. You may be given four alternatives that are almost identical, with only one punctuation or spelling difference.

For example:

Choose the correctly punctuated sentence.

  • A. The teacher said "work hard".
  • B. The teacher said, "Work hard."
  • C. The teacher said "Work hard."
  • D. The teacher, said "Work hard."

Answer: B. The introductory reporting clause is followed by a comma, and the direct quotation begins with a capital letter.

19. Step-by-Step Method for Answering Spelling Questions

  1. Read every option carefully.
  2. Look for differences in vowels, doubled consonants and suffixes.
  3. Check whether the question expects British or American spelling. For JAMB Use of English, be familiar with standard British English.
  4. Check the meaning of the word if similar-looking words are involved.
  5. Eliminate obviously incorrect spellings before selecting the final answer.

20. Step-by-Step Method for Answering Punctuation Questions

  1. Read the complete sentence rather than looking only at the punctuation mark.
  2. Identify the grammatical units in the sentence.
  3. Determine whether the sentence contains a list, direct speech, possession, an introductory phrase, a question or closely related clauses.
  4. Check whether a comma, semicolon, colon, apostrophe or other mark is required.
  5. Read the selected option again to ensure that the entire sentence is grammatically correct.

21. Self-Test

Try these questions before checking the answers.

Question 1: Choose the correctly spelt word.

  • A. accomodation
  • B. accommodation
  • C. acommodation
  • D. accomodation

Answer: B. accommodation.

Question 2: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence.

  • A. Musa said, "I am ready."
  • B. Musa said "I am ready".
  • C. Musa said, "I am ready".
  • D. Musa, said "I am ready."

Answer: A. Musa said, "I am ready."

Question 3: Choose the correct word: The school has a strict set of ______.

  • A. principles
  • B. principals
  • C. principle's
  • D. principal's

Answer: A. principles.

Question 4: Choose the correctly spelt British-English word.

  • A. organisation
  • B. organization
  • C. organnisation
  • D. organisasion

Answer: A. organisation.

Question 5: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?

  • A. However the candidate continued writing.
  • B. However, the candidate continued writing.
  • C. However the candidate, continued writing.
  • D. However, the candidate, continued writing.

Answer: B. However, the candidate continued writing.

22. Quick Revision Summary

  • Full stop (.) — ends a complete statement or command.
  • Comma (,) — separates items, introductory elements and certain clauses or expressions.
  • Semicolon (;) — links closely related independent clauses.
  • Colon (:) — introduces a list, explanation or elaboration.
  • Apostrophe (') — shows possession or omitted letters in contractions.
  • Question mark (?) — ends a direct question.
  • Exclamation mark (!) — expresses strong emotion or emphasis.
  • Quotation marks — indicate direct speech or exact words.
  • Hyphen (-) — joins parts of some compound words.
  • Standard spelling — use accepted spellings consistently, paying particular attention to standard British-English forms expected in Nigerian academic contexts.

23. Examination Reminder

When answering JAMB Use of English questions on punctuation and spelling, do not choose an option simply because it looks familiar. Examine the whole sentence, identify the grammatical purpose of the punctuation or spelling, and then select the option that follows standard English usage.

Frequent revision of commonly confused words, British-English spellings, punctuation rules and practice questions will improve both speed and accuracy.

lessons.subject: english
lessons.title: Sentence Interpretation
lessons.html:
Sentence Interpretation

Sentence interpretation is the ability to understand and correctly explain the meaning conveyed by a sentence. In JAMB Use of English, candidates are required to select the option that best explains the information contained in a given sentence. The correct answer is usually the option that preserves the exact meaning of the original sentence without adding, removing or changing important information.

What JAMB Tests in Sentence Interpretation

Sentence interpretation is part of Lexis and Structure in the JAMB Use of English syllabus. Candidates are expected to understand sentences used in ordinary, figurative and idiomatic contexts and to interpret the information conveyed in them.

The skill therefore goes beyond knowing the dictionary meaning of individual words. You must understand how the words work together in the particular sentence.

How to Interpret a Sentence

When you are given a sentence and four options, use the following procedure:

  1. Read the entire sentence carefully. Do not decide the meaning from one word alone.
  2. Identify the key expression. Look for an idiom, phrasal verb, figurative expression, unusual construction or important grammatical structure.
  3. Determine the context. Ask what is actually happening in the sentence.
  4. Restate the sentence in simple English. Explain what the speaker or writer means without changing the information.
  5. Compare the options. Eliminate choices that introduce information not contained in the original sentence.
  6. Choose the closest equivalent. The correct answer should communicate essentially the same idea as the original sentence.

Literal and Figurative Meaning

A sentence may communicate its meaning literally or figuratively.

Literal meaning is the ordinary or direct meaning of an expression. For example, in the sentence "The boy opened the door," the words have their ordinary meanings.

Figurative meaning occurs when words are used in a non-literal way to express an idea. For example, "The news broke his heart" does not mean that his physical heart was broken. It means that the news caused him great emotional pain.

In JAMB questions, do not interpret a figurative expression word-for-word. Look for the idea represented by the expression.

Idiomatic Expressions

An idiom is an expression whose overall meaning cannot always be obtained by interpreting each word literally. Sentence interpretation questions frequently test the ability to recognise such expressions.

For example:

  • Throw in the towel means to give up or admit defeat.
  • Leave no stone unturned means to make every possible effort.
  • See eye to eye means to agree or have the same opinion.
  • A bolt from the blue means something sudden and unexpected.
  • Put a spoke in someone's wheel means to obstruct or frustrate someone's plans.
  • Turn over a new leaf means to change one's behaviour for the better.
  • Be beside the point means to be irrelevant to the issue under discussion.
  • Bring something home to someone means to make something clear or fully understandable to someone.

When an idiom occurs in a sentence, select the option that gives its established meaning rather than its literal meaning.

Understanding Context

The meaning of a word or expression can depend on the context in which it occurs. The same word may have different meanings in different sentences.

For example, "The chairman addressed the meeting" means that the chairman spoke to the people at the meeting. However, "The chairman addressed the letter" means that he wrote the name and address on the letter.

Therefore, always interpret a word or expression according to the sentence in which it appears.

Interpreting Phrasal Verbs

Phrasal verbs consist of a verb combined with one or more particles, and their meaning may differ from the ordinary meaning of the verb.

  • Give up means to stop trying or surrender.
  • Look after means to take care of.
  • Put off means to postpone.
  • Carry out means to perform or execute.
  • Call off means to cancel.
  • Take after means to resemble a parent or relative.
  • Fall in with can mean to agree with or accept a plan.

In an examination question, replace the phrasal verb mentally with its appropriate meaning and then compare the resulting sentence with the options.

Interpreting Comparisons and Expressions of Degree

Some questions test whether you can correctly understand comparisons, quantities and degrees of difference.

Consider the sentence: "I owe you far less than you owe me."

The important relationship is that both people owe money, but the speaker owes a smaller amount. An option saying that the debts are approximately equal would therefore be incorrect.

Words such as more, less, fewer, greater, hardly, only, almost, never and always can significantly affect meaning. Read them carefully.

Interpreting Negative and Restrictive Expressions

Negative words can easily change the meaning of a sentence. Pay particular attention to expressions such as hardly, scarcely, barely, no sooner, not until and only.

For example, "He had hardly spoken when the bell rang" means that the bell rang almost immediately after he began or finished speaking. It does not mean that he found speaking difficult.

Similarly, "She did not leave until the teacher arrived" means that the teacher arrived before she left.

Interpreting Grammatical Structures

Sometimes the challenge is not an idiom but the grammatical structure of the sentence. Pay attention to tense, voice, conditionals, conjunctions, clauses and the relationship between actions.

For example:

"The letter was being written by the principal."

This is in the passive voice and indicates an action that was in progress at a particular time. The equivalent meaning is that the principal was writing the letter.

Do not select an option that changes the tense or completion of the action.

Interpreting Metaphorical Expressions

A metaphor describes one thing in terms of another in order to communicate an idea vividly.

For example, "His Achilles' heel is pride" does not mean that pride is literally located in his heel. It means that pride is his particular weakness.

Another example is "The issue is a thorn in his flesh." This means that the issue is a persistent source of difficulty, irritation or distress.

Common Idioms and Their Meanings

ExpressionMeaning
Beat about the bushAvoid coming directly to the point
Break the iceMake people feel more relaxed in a new or uncomfortable situation
Burn the midnight oilWork or study late into the night
Cut cornersDo something cheaply or carelessly by avoiding necessary steps
Hit the nail on the headIdentify or express something exactly
In hot waterIn trouble
On the same pageHave the same understanding or opinion
Once in a blue moonVery rarely
Pull someone's legTease or joke with someone
Read between the linesLook for a hidden or implied meaning
Spill the beansReveal a secret
Take the bull by the hornsDeal with a difficult situation boldly
The ball is in your courtIt is now your responsibility to take action
Under the weatherFeeling unwell
Up in armsVery angry or strongly opposed to something

Worked Examples

Example 1: The chairman advised the members not to throw in the towel.

Meaning: The chairman advised the members not to give up.

Why? "Throw in the towel" is an idiomatic expression meaning to surrender or give up.

Example 2: The lecturer's examples brought the theory home to the students.

Meaning: The examples made the theory clear and understandable to the students.

Why? "Bring something home to someone" means to make an idea clear or personally understandable.

Example 3: The accusation was a bolt from the blue.

Meaning: The accusation was sudden and unexpected.

Why? The expression "a bolt from the blue" describes something that happens unexpectedly.

Example 4: The boy accused his friend of putting a spoke in his wheel.

Meaning: The boy accused his friend of obstructing or frustrating his plans.

Why? The expression refers to deliberately creating an obstacle to someone's progress.

Example 5: The students felt the lecture was a load of rubbish.

Meaning: The students thought the lecture was foolish, worthless or nonsensical.

Why? In this context, "a load of rubbish" is figurative and refers to something considered meaningless or of very poor quality.

How to Eliminate Wrong Options

JAMB sentence interpretation questions often contain distractors that look related to the original sentence but do not convey the same meaning. Use these checks:

  • Literal distractor: It interprets an idiom word-for-word.
  • Opposite meaning: It reverses what the sentence says.
  • Partial meaning: It captures only one small part of the sentence.
  • Exaggeration: It introduces a stronger meaning than the original.
  • Unsupported information: It adds facts that are not present in the sentence.
  • Changed tense: It changes whether an action is past, present, future, ongoing or completed.
  • Changed relationship: It changes who performed an action or who received it.

Exam Strategy

  1. Read the sentence twice if necessary.
  2. Underline or mentally identify the key expression.
  3. Ask yourself, "What is the speaker really saying?"
  4. Convert difficult expressions into simple English.
  5. Ignore attractive options that merely repeat words from the question.
  6. Check that the chosen option preserves the same tense, direction, degree and relationship.
  7. When two options appear close, choose the one that explains the complete sentence more precisely.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Do not interpret idioms literally.
  • Do not choose an answer simply because it contains words from the original sentence.
  • Do not ignore negative words such as not, hardly and never.
  • Do not change the tense of the original sentence.
  • Do not assume that a familiar word always has the same meaning in every context.
  • Do not select an option because it sounds reasonable if it does not convey the exact information in the sentence.

Self-Check Practice

Try to interpret each sentence before checking any answer key.

  1. The manager's sudden resignation came as a bolt from the blue. What does this mean?
  2. The students eventually fell in with the teacher's plan. What does this mean?
  3. After several warnings, the boy decided to turn over a new leaf. What does this mean?
  4. The two brothers see eye to eye on the matter. What does this mean?
  5. The chairman's argument was beside the point. What does this mean?

Answers to the Self-Check

  1. The resignation was sudden and unexpected.
  2. The students eventually accepted or agreed with the teacher's plan.
  3. The boy decided to change his behaviour for the better.
  4. The two brothers have the same or similar opinion on the matter.
  5. The chairman's argument was irrelevant to the issue being discussed.

Key Points to Remember

  • Sentence interpretation means identifying the exact information or meaning conveyed by a sentence.
  • The correct option must be equivalent in meaning to the original sentence.
  • Idioms must normally be interpreted according to their established meanings, not literally.
  • Context determines the meaning of many words and expressions.
  • Pay close attention to tense, negation, comparison, degree and grammatical relationships.
  • Eliminate options that change, exaggerate or add information to the original sentence.
  • Regular practice with standard questions improves speed and accuracy.

Final Revision Tip

When faced with a JAMB sentence interpretation question, mentally replace the difficult expression with simple English and then compare that meaning with the four options. The best answer is not necessarily the option that uses the same words as the question; it is the option that communicates the same idea most accurately.

lessons.subject: english
lessons.title: Summary
lessons.html:
Summary and Synthesis of Ideas

Summary questions test your ability to identify and combine the most important ideas in a passage while leaving out unnecessary details. In the JAMB Use of English examination, summary-related questions require you to understand the central ideas of a passage, identify relevant supporting points, make logical deductions and, where necessary, synthesize ideas from different parts of the passage.

What Is a Summary?

A summary is a brief statement of the main ideas contained in a longer passage. It presents the essential information in fewer words without changing the original meaning.

For example, if a passage explains that poor study habits, lack of concentration and inadequate preparation contribute to poor examination performance, a suitable summary may be: Poor preparation and ineffective study habits can lead to poor examination performance.

The summary removes individual examples and combines related ideas into one concise statement.

What JAMB Tests in Summary Questions

Summary questions are closely connected with the comprehension skills required by the JAMB Use of English syllabus. You should be able to:

  • Identify the main point of a passage or paragraph.
  • Recognize important supporting ideas.
  • Distinguish essential information from examples and illustrations.
  • Understand the meaning of words, phrases and sentences as they are used in context.
  • Make logical deductions and inferences from information in a passage.
  • Identify the writer's purpose, attitude or opinion where relevant.
  • Combine related ideas from different parts of a passage.
  • Select a concise statement that accurately represents the ideas in the passage.

Main Idea and Supporting Details

The main idea is the central message or most important point the writer wants the reader to understand. Supporting details explain, prove, illustrate or develop the main idea.

Consider this example:

Many students perform poorly in examinations because they begin preparing only a few days before the examination. Effective preparation requires regular study, revision and adequate rest. Students who organize their study time early are usually better prepared to deal with examination questions.

The central idea is that early and organized preparation improves examination performance. The reference to regular study, revision and rest supports this idea.

Topic Sentence

A topic sentence is a sentence that expresses the main idea of a paragraph. It is often found at the beginning of the paragraph, although it may also occur later or be implied.

When answering summary questions, locating the topic sentence can help you identify the central idea quickly. However, do not assume that the first sentence is always the main point. Read the entire paragraph and determine what all the sentences are discussing.

Essential and Non-Essential Information

Not every detail in a passage belongs in a good summary. You should separate information that is necessary from information that merely illustrates or emphasizes a point.

Essential Information

  • Main arguments.
  • Important causes and effects.
  • Major problems and solutions.
  • Important comparisons or contrasts.
  • Key conclusions.
  • Ideas directly related to the question.

Usually Non-Essential Information

  • Specific examples used to explain a general point.
  • Repeated statements.
  • Decorative descriptions.
  • Minor details.
  • Personal anecdotes that do not answer the question.
  • Information that is unrelated to the question being asked.

Paraphrasing in Summary Questions

To paraphrase means to express an idea using different words while preserving its original meaning. Paraphrasing is useful because JAMB may present the correct answer using words that are different from those in the passage.

For example:

Passage: Regular exercise contributes significantly to physical and mental well-being.

Paraphrase: Consistent physical activity improves both the body and the mind.

The wording is different, but the meaning remains essentially the same.

How to Recognize a Correct Summary

A correct summary should satisfy four important conditions:

  1. Accuracy: It must represent the writer's actual idea.
  2. Completeness: It should include the important points required by the question.
  3. Conciseness: It should avoid unnecessary words and details.
  4. Faithfulness: It must not introduce information or opinions that are absent from the passage.

Synthesis of Ideas

Synthesis means bringing two or more related ideas together to form one clear conclusion. In JAMB comprehension, the information needed to answer a question may appear in different sentences or paragraphs.

For example, a passage may state that:

  • Deforestation destroys natural habitats.
  • It also increases soil erosion.
  • Loss of vegetation can contribute to flooding.

These ideas can be synthesized as: Deforestation causes several environmental problems, including habitat destruction, soil erosion and flooding.

The synthesized statement combines the separate points without adding an unsupported idea.

Cause and Effect in Summary

Many summary questions test your ability to identify relationships between causes and effects.

A cause explains why something happens, while an effect explains what happens as a result.

Look for words and expressions such as because, since, owing to, as a result, therefore, consequently, leads to, results in, causes and due to.

Example:

Passage: Heavy rainfall filled the drainage channels with water. Because the channels could not contain the increased volume, several streets were flooded.

Summary: Excessive rainfall caused flooding because the drainage channels could not contain the water.

Problem and Solution

Another common structure in passages presents a problem followed by one or more solutions.

When summarizing such a passage, identify:

  • What the problem is.
  • What caused or worsened the problem.
  • What solution or solutions the writer proposes.

Do not confuse the problem with its symptoms, and do not select a solution that the passage does not support.

Comparison and Contrast

Some passages compare two people, situations, systems, ideas or objects. A comparison shows similarities, while a contrast shows differences.

Useful signals include similarly, likewise, both, unlike, whereas, while, however, in contrast, on the other hand and although.

When summarizing a comparison, identify the particular feature being compared rather than simply listing unrelated characteristics of the two subjects.

Inference and Implied Meaning

An inference is a conclusion that can reasonably be drawn from information given in the passage. It is not necessarily stated word-for-word.

For example, if a passage says that a student studied consistently throughout the term, attended revision classes and completed several practice tests, you may infer that the student was well prepared for the examination.

A valid inference must be supported by the passage. Avoid choosing an answer simply because it sounds reasonable in real life.

Writer's Purpose and Attitude

Understanding the writer's purpose can help you select the correct summary or inference. A writer may aim to inform, explain, persuade, criticize, advise, warn, describe or entertain.

The writer's attitude refers to the writer's feeling or position towards the subject. It may be positive, negative, critical, sympathetic, doubtful, approving, concerned or neutral.

Always base your interpretation on evidence in the passage rather than on your personal opinion.

A Step-by-Step Method for JAMB Summary Questions

  1. Read the question carefully. Determine exactly what information you are required to identify.
  2. Read the relevant part of the passage. Do not rely on memory alone.
  3. Identify the central idea. Ask yourself what the writer is mainly saying about the subject.
  4. Underline or mentally note key points. Focus on ideas directly related to the question.
  5. Remove unnecessary details. Ignore examples, repetition and minor descriptions unless the question specifically asks about them.
  6. Combine related ideas. If two or more sentences express connected points, mentally bring them together.
  7. Paraphrase where necessary. Look for an option that expresses the same meaning using different words.
  8. Compare the options carefully. Eliminate answers that are incomplete, exaggerated, irrelevant or unsupported.
  9. Choose the most accurate option. The correct answer should represent the passage without changing its meaning.

Common Traps in JAMB Summary Questions

1. The Option That Is True but Not the Answer

An option may contain information that is mentioned in the passage but still fail to answer the specific question. Always return to the question before selecting an answer.

2. The Overly Broad Option

An answer may sound impressive but make a claim that is wider than the passage supports. Avoid answers that generalize beyond the writer's argument.

3. The Incomplete Option

An option may mention one correct point but leave out another major point required by the question. A good answer should cover the essential information.

4. The Distorted Option

Some options use words that subtly change the writer's meaning. Watch for words such as always, never, all, none, only and completely when the passage does not justify such absolute claims.

5. The Personal-Opinion Option

Do not select an answer because you personally agree with it. The answer must be supported by the passage.

6. The Example Trap

An example may be memorable but may not be the main point. When the question asks for the summary or central idea, prefer the general point that the example illustrates.

Worked Example

Passage: Many communities depend on agriculture for food and income. However, declining soil fertility has reduced crop yields in some areas. Farmers can improve productivity by using appropriate organic matter, practising crop rotation and preventing excessive erosion. Access to agricultural education is also important because farmers need to understand how to apply these methods effectively.

Question: What is the main point of the passage?

  1. Agriculture provides food and income to many communities.
  2. Declining soil fertility is responsible for all agricultural problems.
  3. Improving soil management and agricultural knowledge can increase farm productivity.
  4. Farmers should stop using traditional methods of farming.

Answer: C

Explanation: Option C combines the major ideas in the passage: the problem of declining soil fertility and the need for appropriate farming practices and education. Option A is true but focuses only on one supporting detail. Option B exaggerates the passage by saying that declining soil fertility causes all agricultural problems. Option D introduces an idea that the passage does not state.

Another Example of Synthesis

Passage: Reading exposes students to new vocabulary and different styles of expression. It also develops their ability to understand complex arguments. Students who read widely often find it easier to express their ideas clearly because they encounter different ways of organizing information.

Question: Which statement best summarizes the passage?

  1. Reading is the only way students can improve their vocabulary.
  2. Reading widely develops language ability, comprehension and clear expression.
  3. Students who read books always perform better than other students.
  4. Complex arguments are difficult for students who do not read novels.

Answer: B

Explanation: Option B synthesizes the three main benefits mentioned: vocabulary development, better comprehension and clearer expression. The other options either exaggerate the passage or introduce information that was not stated.

Quick Technique for Multiple-Choice Questions

When you are short of time, use the Question–Key Points–Options method.

  1. Question: What exactly is being asked?
  2. Key Points: What two or three ideas in the passage answer it?
  3. Options: Which option combines those ideas accurately and concisely?

This method prevents you from choosing an option simply because it contains familiar words from the passage.

Summary Checklist

  • Have I identified the central idea?
  • Have I focused on information relevant to the question?
  • Have I separated major points from examples?
  • Have I combined related ideas where necessary?
  • Does the answer preserve the writer's meaning?
  • Does the answer avoid unsupported information?
  • Is the answer concise rather than unnecessarily detailed?
  • Have I checked every option against the passage?

Practice Questions

Passage: Public libraries remain valuable even in an age when large amounts of information are available online. Libraries provide access to books, journals and digital resources, while librarians help users evaluate and locate reliable information. They also provide quiet spaces where students and researchers can study. Consequently, libraries continue to support education and independent learning.

Question 1: Which of the following best summarizes the passage?

  1. Libraries are better than the internet for finding information.
  2. Libraries remain important because they provide resources, guidance and spaces for learning.
  3. Students can study only in public libraries.
  4. Librarians are responsible for controlling information on the internet.

Answer: B

Explanation: B combines the three major functions identified in the passage: providing resources, assisting users and providing study spaces.

Question 2: What can be inferred about librarians from the passage?

  1. They write all the books available in libraries.
  2. They help users find and assess information.
  3. They prevent students from using digital resources.
  4. They are responsible for maintaining every educational institution.

Answer: B

Explanation: The passage states that librarians help users evaluate and locate reliable information. Therefore, B is the supported inference.

Final Examination Tips

  • Read for meaning, not merely for individual words.
  • Identify the writer's main argument before examining the options.
  • Pay attention to linking words such as therefore, however, because, although, consequently and in contrast.
  • Do not choose an answer simply because it repeats words from the passage.
  • Prefer an option that accurately combines the major points.
  • Be suspicious of extreme statements unless the passage clearly supports them.
  • Use context to determine meaning rather than relying only on dictionary definitions.
  • For inference questions, choose only conclusions that can be logically supported by the passage.
  • For synthesis questions, look for connections between ideas appearing in different parts of the passage.
  • Manage your time: if an option is clearly unsupported, eliminate it immediately and move to the remaining choices.

Key Takeaway

A successful JAMB summary reader does not try to remember every sentence in a passage. Instead, the reader identifies the main ideas, separates important information from minor details, understands relationships between ideas, makes justified inferences and combines related points accurately. The best summary is therefore accurate, complete, concise and faithful to the passage.
